en: A Compendium of the Essence of the Final Conclusions of All Vedānta.
|| 1 || Homage.
I bow to that Guru Govinda, whose body is consciousness and bliss, by whom the awakening to unbroken bliss arises through salutation and other such acts. (1)
For the attainment of my desired goal, I take refuge in the Self—the unbroken, being-consciousness-bliss, beyond the reach of speech and mind, and the support of all. 2.
When that which one relies upon destroys fear and the arising of obstacles for the virtuous,
then I rely upon that compassionate refuge, the lotus feet of Lambodara.
||2 ||The Fourfold Means of Accomplishment (Sādhanacatuṣṭaya) ||
This compendium of the essence of the established doctrines of the Vedānta scriptures is being spoken for the sake of easily producing understanding among discerning seekers of liberation. (4)
Because this [work] conforms to that treatise, it possesses the fourfold connection (*anubandha-catuṣṭaya*).
That which was specified as the very root of that treatise is now stated here. (5)
The qualified person, the subject matter, the relationship, and the purpose—these they call the fourfold preliminary conditions (anubandha), which constitute the fruit of commencing the treatise. (6)
A person who is fully endowed with the four means of accomplishment, who is skillful in reasoning, intelligent, and learned, is considered qualified for this [task]. (7)
The subject matter is pure consciousness, characterized by the identity of the individual soul and Brahman;
therein alone is found the systematic harmony of all the Vedāntas. (8)

The relationship between this object of knowledge, which is oneness, and its means of knowledge, namely the Śruti, is described by the wise as being characterized by that of the signified and the signifier. (9)
The wise declare that the sole purpose [of this work] is the knowledge of the absolute identity of Brahman and the Self, by which one is instantly liberated from the entire bondage of saṃsāra. (10)
The purpose is the cause for engagement, characterized by its fruit;
for not even a fool engages without aiming at a purpose. (11)
For that wise person who possesses the perfection of the four means of accomplishment, there alone is the attainment of this fruit; for no one else who is deficient in even the slightest degree.
The supreme seers declare that there are four means of accomplishment here;
for liberation is certainly achieved when these exist, and not when they are absent. (13)
The first means [to liberation] is considered to be the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities;
the second is dispassion toward the enjoyment of the fruits of objects here and hereafter. (14)
The perfection of the six qualities beginning with tranquility (śama) is considered the third means;
the fourth means, recognized by the scriptures, is the desire for liberation (mumukṣutva). ||15||
||3 ||Discernment of Reality (Vastuviveka)
The realization that Brahman alone is eternal while everything else is indeed non-eternal—this is what is called the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities. (16)
The cause, such as clay and so forth, is eternal because it is perceived throughout the three periods of time;
whereas its effect, such as a jar and so forth, is non-eternal, since its destruction is observed.
In the same way, this entire world is impermanent because it is an effect of Brahman;
its cause, the Supreme Brahman, must be eternal, like clay and other such materials.
For this reason, the Śruti also says, "From that, indeed, from this [Self], [it] speaks of creation.
Therefore, there is no doubt regarding its impermanence.

Since it is established in every respect that everything is impermanent by virtue of possessing parts, the notion of permanence regarding Vaikuṇṭha and other such realms is merely an illusion of those with deluded intellects. (20)
The discernment of impermanence and permanence through scripture and reasoning in this manner is called the discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal. (21)
||4 ||Freedom from craving.

Indeed, that state of desirelessness which arises from the conviction of impermanence regarding objects pertaining to this world and the next, and which views them with a sense of worthlessness, is called dispassion (vairāgya). ||22||

From the discernment of eternal and non-eternal objects, there immediately arises in a person detachment from everything that is impermanent, such as garlands, sandalwood paste, women, and the like. (23)

An intellect as unbearable as the excrement of a crow toward objects of enjoyment is held to be intense dispassion (*tīvravirakti*). The virtuous say that the very perception of defects in objects of enjoyment is the primary cause for the intensity of such dispassion. (24)
Where a fault is clearly perceived in an object, there is no further engagement with it by a person;
for who indeed would approach even a beautiful courtesan if they knew her to be possessed of a great internal disease? (25)
In this case as well as others, one must simply examine the object that exists;
for by investigating the qualities of an object according to its specific mode, one reveals its very defect. (26)

Reflecting upon dwelling then within the womb amidst the mother's excrement and urine, being bitten by the worms of feces, and being scorched by the fire of her digestive heat—who would not attain detachment? (27)

Who, reflecting upon childhood—when one’s own excrement and urine are discharged, when one lies down on one's back, and when one suffers the blows of child-seizing spirits and the like—would not attain detachment? 28.

Reflecting upon being beaten by one's own or others, a state of ignorance, extreme fickleness, improper conduct, and behavior forbidden during childhood—what person would not turn away from such things? (29)

Who, having reflected upon each of those wicked behaviors arising from intoxication, pride, contempt for those worthy of honor, the state of being afflicted by lust, and the transgression of established conventions, would not turn away from them? (30)

Reflecting upon that deformity, the contempt of all people, the wretchedness everywhere, the deficiency of one's own intellect, and that miserable state brought about by old age—who indeed would not turn away from worldly life? (31)

Who, having reflected upon the intense suffering arising from diseases such as bile-fever, hemorrhoids, consumption, abdominal tumors, colic, and phlegm, as well as foul odors, ill health, and unabated anxiety, would not turn away from worldly life? (32)

Who, having reflected upon the trembling born of fear at the sight of Yama, the agony in the vital organs, the gasping breaths, and the sensations perceived at the departure of life, would not turn away from worldly existence? (33)

Having considered the torment inflicted by the messengers of Yama in the River of Coals, in the Tapanīya hell, in Kumbhīpāka, in Vīci, and in the Forest of Sword-leaves—who would not turn away from worldly life? (34)

When their merit is exhausted, who would not turn away from worldly life upon reflecting on those doers of merit as they fall from the sky, their limbs weakened by the celestial beings, and descend from heaven in the form of constellations? (35)

Having reflected upon the lords of the gods—Vāyu, Arka, Vahni, Indra, and Īśa—whose inner hearts were bound by intense fear of the fierce [Yama], and who were being tormented by their adversaries, who indeed would not turn away from worldly existence? (36)

Having reflected that the gradation of happiness—from Brahmā down to the Great Lord of the Earth—is declared by the Śruti to be merely conditional and not real, who indeed would not turn away from worldly desire? (37)
The distinctions such as *sālokya*, *sāmīpya*, and *sarūpatā* are established through specific virtuous actions;
however, considering that what is accomplished by action cannot be eternal, who would not attain renunciation? (38)

Since there exists in this world a gradation of destinies characterized by high and low states, and since suffering surely exists here as a result of those [destinies], who indeed would not turn away from worldly life upon reflecting on this? (39)
What discerning man in this world would take delight in the perishable and trivial pleasures of home and the like, when he observes that living beings die in vain through delusion? (40)
When investigated, what happiness is there here in a house, or in a woman, or in material objects?
Only those whose eyes are blinded by the darkness of illusion and who are devoid of discernment fall into delusion. (41)
Everything that is pleasing only so long as it is not investigated is like the fruit of the udumbara tree—a mere object of enjoyment.
Ignorance is what is to be enjoyed, but not so for those who possess knowledge, whether in regard to a woman or any other object.

Just as a crab, even when the water has receded, is unable to leave its hole and dies out of delusion, so too a man, through his infatuation, meets with destruction while clinging to the pleasures of the home. 43.
The silkworm, repeatedly wrapping its own body with its threads and desiring protection, becomes utterly unable to emerge by itself; consequently, at the end, it dies clinging to its cocoon. (44)
Just so, the householder, bound by the ties of affection for his children, wife, and friends, is never able to leave his home even after having abandoned them; he dies in vain. (45)
When carefully considered, what difference is seen between this prison and that one?
For here too, a man is turned away from liberation by the bonds of delusion arising from the pleasure of his beloved. (46)
Longing for home is a chain fastened to one's feet; hope for wife and children is a sharp noose around the neck;
the thunderbolt of wealth falling upon the head is indeed the direct cause of the end of life—this craving for riches is truly powerful. 47.
One whose intellect is unattached.
With his feet bound by hundreds of snares of hope, unable even to rise, and being constantly guarded by adversaries such as desire, anger, and pride;
hidden by the veil of delusion within the prison-house of saṃsāra—who among the passionate could possibly be capable of escaping while remaining subject to the threefold cravings? (48)
One whose vision is obstructed by the darkness of desire becomes deluded even regarding the unreal nature of a woman;
for one whose sight is blinded, there is no discernment of whether something is pleasant or painful, regardless of its existence or non-existence. (49)
The mouth oozes with phlegm, the nose drips with foul secretions, the eyes are filled with tears,
and the body all around is exuding sweat, burdened with filth and pervaded by a loathsome stench;
it is something else that can hardly even be described, and the mind ought not to contemplate it at all.
How could such a female form become an object for the eyes of those with refined minds? ||50||

Just as a moth, seeing a flame from afar, perishes by falling upon it through the notion that it is beautiful, so too this man, whose vision is destroyed, how could he perceive the path to liberation? (51)

Just as one who, out of desire, embraces a beloved woman and thus perishes with his vision destroyed, so too does this person—seeing a woman, who is merely a vessel of flesh, bone, marrow, filth, and urine, as being inherently delightful—come to ruin through his lost discernment. (52)
Desire itself is Yama manifest; the beloved woman is the Vaitaraṇī river; but for the seeker of liberation who possesses discernment, the abode of Yama is his own home.
Neither in the abode of Yama nor even in their own homes is there any cessation of the affliction of the threefold suffering for men;
yet, perceiving only a slight respite from it, the foolish world regards itself as being of the nature of happiness. (54)
When the relative degree of Yama and Kāma is considered, there is a great difference between them in this world:
Yama, though unpleasant, does what is beneficial for one; Kāma, however, causes harm even while being pleasant. (55)
Yama brings misfortune only to the wicked, while he, being benevolent, bestows happiness upon the virtuous;
likewise, Kāma obstructs the path only of the virtuous and brings misfortune to them—so what need is there to mention the wicked? ||56||
Desiring the increase of the universe himself, he created the lustful person as its impeller;
by that very person, the world, becoming utterly infatuated, increases just as the ocean does through the moon. ||57||

Desire, the great agitator of the world, having itself entered within the inner self of both man and woman, clearly manifests through laughter and various emotional states arising from the qualities of their mutual limbs;
having utterly deluded one another with its own darkness and the bond of passion, it binds them both.
Having bound it, he whirls it about, increasing the fabrication of conceptual proliferation like a slayer of a Brahmin. //58//
Therefore, since the impulse of desire resides within as an internal factor, engagement with objects of enjoyment is established by itself;
for otherwise, how could every living being engage with objects that have not been made known? (59)
For that very reason, the desire of all living beings is most powerful;
even as this body decays, desire itself does not decay.
Having perceived the fault in sense objects, the wise person endowed with discernment who is released from the snare of desire is one who moves upon the path of liberation.
I shall declare to the virtuous the subtle means for conquering desire;
the renunciation of mental construction (saṃkalpa) is considered the easily attainable means. (62)
Whether the object of enjoyment be heard of or seen, regarding whatever thing it may be,
desire never arises at any time due to the abandonment of the notion that it is desirable.
Volition is the seed of desire; it arises from volition alone. When that [volition] is destroyed, desire perishes like a sprout when its seed is destroyed. ||64||

No man is capable of desiring that which is to be experienced as an object of enjoyment without the intellect of right conviction (*samyaktva*); therefore, one who desires to conquer passion should destroy this [desire] by means of the intellect of right conviction regarding sense objects. (65)
A person desiring to conquer desire regarding objects of enjoyment should destroy the notion of pleasure inherent in sense-objects;
for as long as the deluded intellect perceives pleasure in a thing, one will certainly not be able to conquer desire.

The cause for the non-arising of conceptual construction is the vision of things as they truly are, and the contemplation of their lack of intrinsic reality; through these two, no opportunity for such construction exists. (67)

If, regarding a jewel, the notion that it is a mere stone arises, or if fear thereof occurs, then neither the cognition of its excellence nor the cognition of its worthiness to be acquired will arise. (68)
Since the perception of an object as beneficial leads one to contemplate even what is harmful, that very contemplation is considered a means for the destruction of desire itself. (69)
Freedom from greed.

Wealth is the cause of fear, the constant increase of suffering, and an extremely fierce torment; it causes the estrangement of kinsmen and the cultivation of a base intellect; it is an obstacle to distinguished virtues and the means by which the wretched-minded are gratified.
It is neither a means for attaining liberation, nor is it a purifier of the heart. ||70||
For a king, there is fear from thieves, fear arising from negligence, and in reality, fear from his own kinsmen;
wealth is seized by fear and is the root of misfortune—it does not lead to happiness for the virtuous. (71)
In reality, for men, there is always only suffering in the acquisition, protection, giving away, or even the expenditure of wealth; wealth is not a means to happiness.
Even for the virtuous, greed increases through the acquisition of objects;
discernment is destroyed by greed, and when that is lost, one perishes. (73)
In the absence of gain, greed burns one who is devoid of acquisitions; when gain is present, greed burns that very person.
Therefore, how can wealth, which causes such torment, ever bestow happiness? (74)
For a living being, intoxication comes from enjoyment, while rebirth results from giving;
thus wealth is rendered useless in both cases, for there is no other way [to achieve liberation]. (75)
Through wealth there is an increase of intoxication; through intoxication comes the destruction of memory;
from the destruction of memory comes the destruction of intellect; and from the destruction of intellect, one perishes. (76)
The foolish world, dull-witted and firmly embraced by the demoness of inner hope that "wealth alone brings happiness," dwells constantly at its edge, gazing [only] toward it.
Even that [wind] departs afterwards, having taken away his vital breath.
Though fully endowed with sight, he sees nothing else with his eyes as if he were blind; he walks only upon paths shunned by the virtuous, encouraged by fools.
Repeatedly stumbling at every step upon that very path, he falls into a blind well; poverty alone is the collyrium that serves as the medicine to remove this blindness. (78)
Greed, anger, hypocrisy, pride, and envy indeed increase with the acquisition of wealth; how then can that be a purification of the mind? (79)
The suffering that arises from the expenditure of wealth is twice as great as the suffering from not obtaining it;
for even the wise, the suffering from its misappropriation is three times greater than that. (80)
How can there be peace of mind for a householder with wealth that is constantly maintained and never free from fear and anxiety, any more than there is for one who dwells with a snake? (81)
Whether in a wilderness, a lonely forest, a populated district, on a bridge, or in a desolate place;
whether accompanied by other excellent men or even separated from them;
whether destitute or otherwise—he dwells happily with a sense of well-being, respected by the people.
The wealthy man is always afflicted by a troubled mind and is even afraid of his own son. //82//
Therefore, wealth is the cause of misfortune; by means of it, the accomplishment of the goals of human life does not occur.
Consequently, the virtuous dwell at the edge of the forest, having renounced all wealth that is adverse to their well-being. (83)

Having realized through the declarations of the Vedas and through reasoning that everything is perishable—possessing a virtuous wife endowed with faith, devotion, and wisdom; sons who are learned and esteemed; inexhaustible wealth and the splendor of earthly enjoyments; and a beautiful mansion—wise poets renounce it all. Others, however, deluded by the thought that this is happiness, wander in the ocean of suffering. (84)

Those who, like worms in this house, take pleasure in the mass of impurities through attachment to wife, field, and son—thinking it to be happiness—have no possibility of liberation, as if they were in the realm of the gods; rather, for them there is only a continuous flow of suffering from dwelling in the womb of hell. (85)
For those whose hope for wives, children, wealth, and the like has become hopeless, their path directed toward the hope of liberation succeeds; it does not succeed for others.
For those who have destroyed their sins through virtuous deeds, who possess learning, whose souls are perfected, and who are wise;
for those who repeatedly employ reasoning to purify the categories of eternal and non-eternal objects;
and for those who, possessing the sword of great dispassion arising from that [purification], desire only liberation—[for them, this work is intended].
For the fortunate, it is easy to sever the creeping vine of desire regarding objects such as women and the like. (87)
There are three great doors through which the powerful Death of saṃsāra enters the world: women, the tongue, and gold. He who blocks these has no fear of death. (88)
The first gate of the city of Muktiśrī, which is most difficult to conquer, has two door-panels— wealth and a young woman— which fasten it firmly together.
This triad—the door and the formidable bolt of Kāmākhyā—is powerful; the steadfast man who breaks through it is worthy to enjoy the glory of liberation. 89.
For one who has mounted the horse of discernment, who wields the sword of intense dispassion, and is clad in the armor of forbearance, no adversary is seen. (90)
The wise declare that intense detachment born of discrimination alone is the primary cause of liberation;
therefore, the seeker of liberation who possesses discrimination should cultivate renunciation.
One should first accomplish that with diligent effort. ||91||
A person who has not yet developed world-weariness is indeed unable to cast off the bondage of the body; for that world-weariness is the great shatterer of bondage.
Lacking detachment, even those who are learned suffer from the three kinds of torments within their dwellings, as if in the abode of Yama, though they are deluded. (93)
Tranquility, self-control, forbearance, renunciation, faith, and thereafter concentration—these six alone are declared to be tranquility and the rest. (94)
Peace.
The steady abiding of the mind upon its own object through single-pointed application alone is called *śama* (tranquility) by the virtuous who know the characteristics of tranquility. (95)
It is classified in three ways—as superior, middling, and inferior—by the wise who are knowers of their respective characteristics. ||96||
Abandoning its own modifications and abiding as the mere reality of things—this is the supreme peace of the mind, characterized by the nirvana of Brahman. (97)
The continuous flow of the stream of internal cognitions is the function of the intellect;
this is the intermediate state of peace, characterized solely by pure *sattva*. (98)
Having abandoned engagement with sense objects, the mind remains one-pointedly fixed on hearing;
this tranquility of the mind, characterized solely by pure sattva, is the state of "otherness" (itara). 99.
When both the eastern and northern limbs are present, tranquility (*śama*) is accomplished; not otherwise.
Intense dispassion (*virakti*) is the eastern limb, while self-restraint (*dama*) and the others are the northern limbs. (100)
Lust, anger, greed, pride, delusion, and envy—peace is not attained for one by whom these six have not been conquered. (101)
For that mendicant who does not turn away from objects such as sound, which are like poison, even with an intense desire for liberation, peace is not accomplished.
For one who has not propitiated the Lord, for whom there is no favor from the Guru, and whose heart is not under control—for such a person, peace is not attained. (103)
Clarity of mind.
O wise ones, listen to the means for achieving clarity of mind—that which is established when sattva is present, and which does not succeed when it is absent. (104)
Celibacy, non-violence, compassion toward all beings, straightforwardness, extreme lack of craving for sense objects, purity, and the avoidance of hypocrisy. ||105||
Truthfulness, freedom from the sense of "mine," steadfastness, the relinquishing of egoism, devotion to meditation on the Lord, and dwelling together with those who know Brahman. ||106||
Devotion solely to the science of knowledge, equanimity toward pleasure and pain, lack of attachment to honor, constant virtuous conduct, and the desire for liberation. ||107||
The mind of one who possesses all of this becomes serene; but for one devoid of this Dharma, it does not become so even by millions of other means. (108)
Recollection, seeing, praising the qualities and actions of women, the notion that they are excellent, affection for them, and private conversation with them—[these are the causes of passion]. (109)
They know that cohabitation and sexual union are eightfold; celibacy, which is the opposite of this, brings clarity to the mind. (110)
Non-violence is the non-infliction of suffering upon any living being through speech, mind, or body;
regarding all creatures as one’s own self, by means of body, mind, and voice. (111)
Compassion is indeed said by the knowers of Vedānta to be mercy;
it is considered to be the state of being uniform and straightforward across the three instruments [of action]. (112)
That dispassion toward objects which follows along [throughout] from Brahmā down to the level of stationary beings—just like the dispassion felt toward a crow’s excrement—is indeed stainless. (113)
Purity is said to be of two kinds: external and internal.
Purity performed with earth and water is known as external, pertaining to the body. (114)
The removal of ignorance is the internal purity of the mind; when internal purity is properly established, external purification is not necessary for men. (115)
He who performs acts such as meditation and worship in this world merely for the sake of being seen by others, lacking the wisdom of ultimate reality, is said to be one of hypocritical conduct. (116)
The wise know that for a man, non-transgression and freedom from hypocrisy consist in speaking only of that which has been personally seen and properly heard. (117)
Brahman is called "Truth," and speaking of it as "Truth" means the relinquishing of the firm conviction of ownership regarding the body and other such things. (118)
That by which the wise man attains liberation is known as freedom from the sense of "mine";
it is a firm standing in the ascertained meaning through the words of the Guru and the Vedānta. (119)
Stability in that [state] consists in its single-pointed persistence and immovability, and not in the body, nor in learning, power, austerity, form, lineage, caste, stage of life, and so forth. (120)
The abandonment of the arisen ego-sense is the relinquishing of self-conceit; having properly abandoned worldly activity through the three instruments [of body, speech, and mind]. (121)
That which is the contemplation of one's own Self alone is called meditation upon the Lord; it is a constant dwelling like a shadow, the abiding together with those who know Brahman. 122.

Whoever among these is devoted to whatever has been taught in the science of knowledge, such as hearing and so forth, being devoid of the notion of ritual action, he alone is truly established in knowledge. 123.

When the time for wealth, a beloved, fever, and so forth has arrived, there should be freedom from agitation through equanimity toward pleasure and pain; this is indeed the state of being unaffected by such changes.
"Knowing me to be the most excellent and worthy of worship, may people on earth honor me"—the absence of attachment arising from such [desire] is called non-attachment to honor. (125)
Therefore, since this reflection is a confinement and an obstacle in a solitary place, if one remains [therein] alone, that itself is the state of being devoted to solitude. 126.
"When will my liberation from the bonds of saṃsāra occur suddenly?"—this firm resolve that is expressed is called the desire for liberation (mumukṣutā). ||127||

Those who are experts in the meaning of the word *dama* say that "taming" (*dama*) is the restraining of the mind by means of practices such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*) for the sake of removing its defects. (128)
The restraint of the external senses through the cessation of their respective functions is called *dama* (self-control) for the yogi; it is the means for achieving peace of mind. 129.
When the senses engage with their objects by chance, the mind runs after them alone, just as fire follows the wind. (130)
When the sense-faculties have ceased and the mind itself has abandoned its impetuous force, it assumes the state of pure being; through this, clarity arises.
When his mind has become serene, liberation is accomplished; not otherwise. ||131||
The very cause of mental clarity is the restraint of all the sense-faculties;
for when the external senses are properly restrained, [the mind becomes clear].
The mind is detached from the enjoyment of external objects. ||132||
By means of that, having completely abandoned one's own wickedness, the mind gradually attains peace;
this is precisely the liberation of the mind from external objects.
Those who know the defining characteristics of liberation understand liberation [to be such]. ||133||
We know of no means for a seeker of liberation to easily attain the clarity of mind that is the cause of goodness without self-restraint;
through self-restraint, having cast off the multitude of one's own defects, the mind quickly attains peace. (134)
From breath control (prāṇāyāma) arises the steadiness and clarity of the mind;
and even for one who observes specific directions, places, times, and so forth,
that self-restraint is never destroyed by any [distraction], provided it is accompanied by right vision.
The wise person, self-controlled and free from laziness, should strive diligently for the sake of peace of mind.

By restraining the movement of all the senses, by reflecting upon the defects and other faults in objects of enjoyment, and through the grace of the Lord and the grace of the Guru, the mind attains peace before long. (136)
Whatever internal or other suffering has been encountered through the force of *prārabdha* karma, the endurance of that without anxiety is called *titikṣā*. ||137||
For one who seeks liberation, there exists no protection equal to forbearance; it cannot be pierced even by the thunderbolt.
Like a warrior clad in armor, the wise, treating all obstacles as mere straw, conquer illusion by means of that very forbearance.
For it is only for those who possess forbearance that there is the accomplishment of yoga, the attainment of the bliss of sovereignty and the splendor of self-rule;
those devoid of forbearance fall through obstacles, like heaps of leaves struck from a tree by the winds. (139)
Through endurance, austerity, charity, sacrifice, pilgrimage, vows, and sacred learning, prosperity, heaven, and liberation are attained by those who seek them respectively. (140)
Celibacy, non-violence, and not censuring even the virtuous—these are accomplished only by one who possesses endurance (*titikṣu*), such as by bearing insults and the like from others. (141)
Among all spiritual practices, forbearance is the supreme means;
by it, even divine and elemental obstacles flee away. (142)
Only for the patient one whose mind does not turn back from obstacles do all the supernatural powers, such as *aṇimā* and the other prosperities, attain fulfillment. (143)
Therefore, for one who desires liberation, great endurance must be cultivated to accomplish the desired goal; likewise,
there must be an intense longing for liberation and a profound indifference toward worldly things.
Both are auxiliary causes for forbearance. ||144||

If that mendicant, having become intent on the thought of [remedying] the multitude of diseases that arise at various times, were to apply himself to the practice of specific medicinal remedies for their avoidance,
and thus, becoming devoid of the dharma of hearing [the teachings] and so forth, should die; then—
What accomplished fruit could he obtain? In either case, he would fall away from his own purpose. ||145||
"Keśava spoke as follows regarding a monk who practices yoga but whose mind has strayed from it: 'Having reached the worlds of those who perform meritorious deeds,' and so forth. (146)

But the Blessed One does not say that one attains the state of the worlds of merit merely by performing renunciation and then dying in silence; rather, he speaks of it through the mere act of renunciation itself. (147)
Nor does one attain perfection through mere renunciation alone;
thus he stated that there is an absence of perfection resulting from the abandonment of what ought to be performed. (148)

Therefore, having endured each respective suffering that has arisen through patience, one should gradually perform the hearing [of the scriptures] and other practices according to one's capacity. ||149||
The purpose of fortitude, when successfully cultivated through effort, is seen to be that nothing whatsoever remains when one is unable to endure suffering. (150)
||9 ||Renunciation ||
The renunciation, according to the prescribed rule, of all actions that have been perceived as means to an end—that is considered by the wise to be *saṃnyāsa*. (151)

Renunciation (*nyāsa*) is described by the term *uparati* because it brings actions to a halt; for by renunciation, the abandonment of all improper actions (*vikarman*) is proclaimed by the Śruti. (152)

Since it is heard in scripture that impermanence belongs to that which is being accomplished by action, what use is this action for one who desires the eternal fruit and seeks the ultimate reality? (153)

That which is to be produced, that which is to be obtained, that which is to be refined, and that which is to be transformed—these are reckoned as the fourfold results achievable through action; there is nothing beyond these. (154)
Neither of these two can ever be Brahman; for Brahman is self-established, eternally attained, pure, stainless, and inactive. (155)
Nor is it denied by scripture that there is anyone who produced this [Brahman];
therefore, Brahman is the cause, and for that reason, Brahman is not held to be something produced. (156)
If there were a distinction between the attainer and that which is attained, then the attainer would attain what is to be attained;
however, this Brahman is the very nature of the attainer itself and is never something to be attained.
In this world, purification is desired only for things that are already stained, such as a mirror;
for Brahman, who is eternally pure like space, there is no purification whatsoever. (158)
With what defilement could a reality that is stainless and inactive be joined, such that a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) might remove the fault that has arisen through connection with it? (159)
Even the attribution of qualities to that which is devoid of qualities is not at all tenable,
because it is heard in scripture that [Brahman] is "alone" and "devoid of qualities," and thus possesses the state of being without qualities (nairguṇya).
A substance such as milk, which possesses parts and is subject to transformation, may undergo modification by whatever means; but this is not the case for a substance that is devoid of action.
"Partless, actionless, tranquil, blameless, and stainless—such is the true nature of reality, established by both scripture and reasoning. (162)
Therefore, Brahman cannot be accomplished by action through any means whatsoever;
for that which is accomplished by action is indeed impermanent, whereas Brahman is eternal and everlasting.
Just as the body and so forth perish in this world, so too does the world of the hereafter, which has been accumulated through meritorious action, [perish]. (164)
The state of being produced always remains awake as the reason for impermanence;
therefore, what wise person indeed would be deluded regarding heaven and other such things, which are impermanent? (165)
The eternality of that which is the cause of the world is agreed upon by everyone;
yet the Śruti repeatedly declares that this [Īśvara] alone is the cause of the world. (166)
The Śruti, stating "All this has that as its self" and "That is the Truth," clearly declares the eternity of this very Being (sat), which is the cause of the world. (167)
"Neither by action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth"—thus the Śruti itself directly negates that action is a cause of liberation. (168)
Without first investigating the inward Brahman and thereby realizing the oneness of both, liberation—characterized by the state of being the Supreme Brahman itself—is not achieved for the person;

nor is it attained through ritual baths, nor through recitations of praise, nor through mutterings of prayers, nor through the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances, nor even through sacrifices, offerings, gifts, and the study of the Vedas, nor indeed through mantras and tantras. (169)
"But liberation comes from knowledge alone," so it is declared by the Śruti;
that knowledge is the cause of liberation is established through the exclusion of other [causes]. (170)

For one who is discerning, dispassionate, and who knows the eternity of Brahman, how could there be delight in the collection of means for impermanent objects, when he desires that [eternal] state? (171)
Therefore, all action—whether obligatory (*nitya*) or occasional (*naimittika*), along with its means—is enjoined as a means for attaining [results] such as heaven, which are impermanent. (172)
One who desires liberation and seeks the state of Brahman must renounce [worldly action];
yet for the seeker of liberation, ritual action as well as hearing [the scriptures] remains a means. (173)
These two hands will accomplish their own task for him, just as a lamp shines forth through the act of straightening [its wick]. (174)

Just as the awakening of a person arises from hearing [the teachings] through the performance of prescribed rites, therefore knowledge is dependent [on other factors], or else there is a combination [of means]. (175)
The exponents of Brahman declare that this is the means for liberation;
yet how can renunciation be appropriate for one who desires liberation while still performing prescribed duties? (176)
Thus, the best of the wise should not entertain such doubts like the ignorant;
for the fruit of ritual action is one thing, while the fruit of hearing [the scriptures] is distinct. (177)
And there is a difference between the two causal complexes (sāmagrī) in both cases:
one who possesses desire is qualified for ritual action, while one who is free from desire is considered qualified for hearing [the scriptures]. (178)
The characteristics such as "being desirous" and "being capable" are considered for the ritualist;
the characteristics such as "having examined the worlds" are for the seeker of liberation. (179)
The one entitled to liberation is the renunciant (saṃnyāsī), while the householder indeed engages in ritual action (karman).
The means for that action consists of the acceptance of a wife and the sacrificial implements, such as the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles. (180)
For one who desires to hear [the Dharma], there is no need for other means apart from the Guru;
yet, in the absence of the Guru, the egoism increases ever further through one's actions. (181)
The cessation of egoism occurs moment by moment through hearing;
the scripture of action is that which impels, while the scripture of knowledge is that which turns one away from it. 182.
Such is the reversal [of the relationship] regarding that proof and its two subjects;
there is never any mutual dependence between the two. (183)
In the same way, between these two causal complexes, cognition leads [the soul] upward, while ritual action causes it to descend. (184)
How are they mutually dependent, or how are they combined? It is like [the relationship] between fire and a heap of grass, or between light and darkness. (185)
In the same way, the association of knowledge and action is not possible;
for what benefit could action provide to knowledge, which is its own opposite?
By whose mere presence it does not attain manifestation of its own accord. ||186||
Just as fire, even when blazing upon a mountain of ten million loads of fuel,
is not able to assist the sun even slightly,
so too are ten million times a thousand karmas [incapable of assisting the sun].
Does knowledge indeed dissolve by itself? ||187||
Both hands, having a single agent as their substratum, are both authorized for an action; thus, their association is appropriate, but it is not so with knowledge and action. 188.
An agent is able to perform, not perform, or even perform an action otherwise;
however, the cognition of an object is never dependent on the agent in that way.
Just as the object exists, so is the cognition produced by means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
And he does not depend upon any action whatsoever, nor upon skill in reasoning. //190//
If cognition were dependent solely upon the object, how could doubt and the like arise?
Therefore, the wise should not suspect that cognition is not real. (191)
Doubt and the like, which arise when the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) are deficient, are not real;
when the means of valid cognition are excellent, as in the case of the Veda, knowledge becomes real.
The reality is indeed the Supreme Brahman—eternal, true, constant, and all-pervading;
knowledge of that arises solely from the authority of the Śruti, being entirely independent [of other means]. (193)
Just as the knowledge of form arises when right view is present, so too does authentic knowledge arise only when the authority of scripture is present. (194)
For the eye does not depend on any action whatsoever for a person’s perception of form;
likewise, knowledge produced by hearing and so forth [does not depend on action].
In the illumination of an object, it is indeed independent. ||195||
Action depends upon the agent; auspicious and inauspicious results depend upon action;
consciousness depends upon the means of valid cognition; and this world depends upon illusion. (196)
This joint mention of "knowledge and ignorance" has been employed by the wise for the sake of ritual action and meditative worship, but never for the sake of self-knowledge and ritual action. (197)

Action is prescribed by the Śruti for this very dull-witted person who lacks understanding of the categories of the eternal and the non-eternal, whose heart is attached to the experience of objects such as garlands and the like in both worlds, and whose intellect is despondent; it is not, however, enjoined for the wise seeker of liberation who desires supreme bliss and is completely dispassionate. (198)
On the very day that one becomes dispassionate through the desire for liberation, renunciation (nyāsa) is ordained for that wise seeker of liberation;
this is established by that very same supreme Śruti, and therefore by the learned.
One must resolve in one's mind that "this is authoritative. ||199||
The Blessed One himself also negates the efficacy of the Vedas and other such means for one who has attained direct realization, stating:
"Neither by the Vedas, nor by austerity," and so forth. (200)
Both engagement and withdrawal are within the scope of the sacred scriptures:
by engagement a living being is bound, but by withdrawal one is liberated. (201)
Since even a fool does not consider his own kinsmen as his true bond anywhere, therefore renunciation of action must be performed by those who desire liberation. ||202||
Since the simultaneous conjunction of knowledge and action is not tenable, one who desires knowledge must certainly abandon action with effort. (203)
Even for an object grasped through the cognition that it is a means to achieve a desired end, once its worthlessness has been realized, who would ever look toward it again? (204)
For the meaning of the word *uparati* (cessation) is the stopping of previously observed mental modifications;
this [cessation] possesses a twofold nature through its function, being both primary (*mukhya*) and secondary (*gauṇa*). ||205||
The abandonment of the visible world through the cessation of mental activity is said to be the primary meaning;
the renunciation of action is considered the secondary meaning, regarded as a subsidiary element of the sacred scriptures. (206)
For the sake of accomplishing the primary rite, the recourse to its auxiliary parts must certainly be made;
for if the primary rite is devoid of its auxiliaries, it will not be accomplished at all. (207)
One who is thoroughly detached should renounce for the sake of happiness in this world and the next;
for one who is not detached, renunciation is fruitless, like a sacrifice performed by one unworthy to offer it.
Having renounced, the ascetic should not harbor memories of former objects of attachment;
for as he recalls each of those things, a sense of loathing arises within him. (209)

That conviction regarding the words of the Guru and the Vedānta which is of the nature of certainty, thinking "this alone is the truth," is faith; it is the primary cause for the attainment of liberation. (210)
The goal of human life is said to be accomplished only for those who possess faith, and not for others;
thus has the extremely subtle reality of the supreme truth been declared.
And the Veda says, "Have faith in Soma. ||211||
But for one devoid of faith there is no engagement;
for one empty of engagement there is no accomplishment of what is to be achieved.
And all are struck down by faithlessness alone.
They drown in the great ocean of saṃsāra. ||212||

To whatever extent faith arises within a person toward the divine, the Veda, the guru, the mantra, the sacred ford, the high-souled one, and even medicine, to that same extent does spiritual accomplishment arise for men. (213)
It must be apprehended as "it exists," because of the certainty regarding the actual existence of the entity;
that certainty of its existence arises through faith established by the scriptures. (214)
Therefore, faith in the teacher and the words of the Vedānta must be well-established;
for one who desires liberation and possesses faith, the fruit is accomplished, and not otherwise.
Speaking in accordance with reality is the cause for generating faith in persons;
since the Veda is the word of God, there is no doubt regarding its truthfulness. (216)
Since the liberated one possesses the nature of the Lord, the speech of the Guru is likewise such;
therefore, the faithful confidence in his words is established for the wise among the virtuous. (217)
||11 ||The Perfect Installation.
The thorough fixing of the mind upon the object of knowledge for the sake of penetrating the meaning declared by the scriptures is called *samādhi*. (218)
The mind’s exclusive dedication to the single goal to be accomplished is the necessary cause for the attainment of the human aim;
otherwise, the goal is not achieved at all, and even a slight lapse of mental heedfulness renders effort fruitless. (219)
For the one who pierces the target fixes the mind, the vision, and likewise another instrument upon a single point;
just as when there is even a slight lapse on the part of the target-piercer, the discharge of the arrow becomes fruitless. ||220||
The concentration of the mind is the uncommon cause of spiritual accomplishment;
therefore, those who desire liberation must always practice this.
Extreme detachment and a great desire for the fruit—one should know that both of these are the causes of meditative concentration. ||222||
Scripture declares that external factors such as celibacy and the like lead to liberation;
however, the wise know that this group of six, beginning with tranquility (śama), is the internal factor.
Since the internal is indeed stronger than the external,
the seeker of knowledge must necessarily possess the six internal qualities, beginning with tranquility (śama).
For one who lacks internal discipline, even millions of scriptural hearings bear no fruit, just as a warrior lacking fortitude finds that his mastery of weapons is of no avail.
12. The state of desiring liberation (mumukṣutva).

When a wise person, through the knowledge of the oneness of Brahman and the Self, desires to be released from the bondage of the snares of saṃsāra, that is declared to be the state of seeking liberation (mumukṣutva). ||226||
For all spiritual practices, however, the desire for liberation is the root cause.
For one who lacks this desire and does not engage [in practice], where is the scripture, and where indeed is its fruit? (227)
The desire for liberation is of four kinds, distinguished as intense, moderate, mild, and very mild; its various types shall also be proclaimed—let it be heard by the wise. (228)
Constantly tormented by the three kinds of suffering in their many forms, his inner self agitated,
he regarded all possessions as a source of misfortune.
That most intense desire for liberation abandons [all else]. ||229||
Having observed the three intense afflictions and seeing that one must abandon wife and children,
that which is the churning of oneself between these two states— this is the reality.
This very desire for liberation is considered to be the Madhyamika [desire]. ||230||

"There is still time for liberation; why this haste for me today? Having accomplished all my duties through devotion alone, I shall strive for liberation hereafter"—this very mindset is called dull-witted longing for liberation (mumukṣā). (231)
"If I were to obtain a jewel while traveling on the road, then I would be blessed if I were to attain liberation"—
such is the mindset of those with deluded intellects, born of such an expectation.
This very desire for liberation is considered extremely dull.
Having propitiated the Lord through ascetic penance over many thousands of births,
he has thereby completely shaken off all impurities residing within his heart.

One who knows the scriptures, understands virtues and faults, is free from desire for all that is merely enjoyable, knows the nature of eternal and non-eternal things, desires liberation, and is firm in his vows; ||234||
Just as one quickly leaves a vessel that has been heated by fire after setting it aside,
so too does the twice-born man leave his home with an intense longing for liberation.
He alone crosses over transmigratory existence immediately through the grace of the Guru;
he who possesses an intense desire for liberation is liberated even while living. (236)
The middling one [is liberated] in another birth, while the other [the inferior one] is liberated at the end of a *yuga*;
the fourth may be liberated after ten million *kalpas*, or he is not liberated from bondage at all. ||237||
They know that human birth is extremely difficult for a living being to attain; more difficult than that is manhood, and more difficult still is discernment.
Having obtained this triad, a great-souled person, becoming suddenly dispassionate, should strive for liberation. (238)
In birth after birth, the happiness of sons, friends, wives, and so forth, as well as human status, manhood, and discernment, are not obtained. (239)

Having obtained a human birth, which is most difficult to attain, and having therein acquired manliness as well as the discernment between the good and the bad, if one should remain intent on worldly pleasures, then shame on the birth of that evil-minded person, the lowest of men! (240)
The dog, the pig, and the donkey always eat and revel;
what distinction is there between them and those whose livelihood is the same as theirs? (241)
As long as disease has not taken hold, as long as old age has not overtaken him, as long as his intellect does not falter, and as long as he has not beheld death. ||242||
At that very moment, a person who is healthy, intent on grasping the essence, and possessed of discernment should strive swiftly for liberation from the bonds of worldly existence. (243)
Tens of millions have indeed been liberated from the bonds of gods, sages, ancestors, and mortals;
yet whoever is liberated from the bond of worldly existence is the best among the knowers of Brahman.
For one who is bound by an internal bond, what is the use of releasing external bonds? Therefore, let the wise perform that action which leads to liberation from the internal bond. 245.
Intense desire for liberation is considered to culminate only in action;
any other [desire] is a mere coloring of the mind, wherein no action is observed. (246)

The constant and very firm haste of women who, having abandoned their homes and all else with a sense of lightness and a desire for happiness, wish to enter the fire with their husbands— [that haste is the power of the Lord].
This very [discipline] is the instrument for one desiring liberation in reaching the culmination of the fruit. ||247||
Discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal, the realization of the momentariness of the body,
fear of death, and the sense of distress are the causes for the increase of the desire for liberation.
Discrimination is said to be its head, and extreme dispassion its body;
tranquility and the other [five] are its six limbs, while the desire for liberation is held to be its life-breath. (249)
One who is endowed with such qualities, being inquisitive and skilled in reasoning, is truly a hero who certainly slays death with the sword of perfect knowledge. (250)

Endowed with the aforementioned means of accomplishment, the seeker who desires to know the Self should go to a guru for the sake of inquiry, carrying fuel in his hand, disciplined, and radiant. (251)
One who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), established in Brahman, profoundly tranquil, and possessed of equal vision;
who is free from the sense of "mine," free from egoism, free from the pairs of opposites, and free from possessions;
who is indifferent to worldly concerns, pure, skillful, and an ocean of the nectar of compassion.
Endowed with such characteristics, that guru is the foremost among the knowers of Brahman.
He should be approached with effort by one who desires to know for the sake of accomplishing their own goal. ||253||
Propitiated through hundreds of lifetimes by devotees with constant, respectful devotion according to the Vedic injunctions, the Lord himself, being fully satisfied,
has come in person to the venerable Guru and, out of grace, has become visible to his sight.
Having thoroughly awakened [others] to reality, it delivers them from the ocean of the suffering of saṃsāra. ||254||
Since through him there occurs even the liberation from the knot of the heart consisting of ignorance, those who know the true meaning of the word "guru" call him alone the guru. (255)
Śiva alone is the Guru manifest, and the Guru himself is Śiva.
Those seeking liberation should not perceive even the slightest difference between the two. (256)
One should serve a guru who is liberated from bondage, established in Brahman, and has accomplished all that was to be done;
by whose grace the ocean of saṃsāra becomes like the water in a cow's hoofprint.
Having approached a gracious guru with constant service, devotion, prostrations, and humble speech, one should inquire about that which is to be known by oneself. (258)
O Blessed One, ocean of compassion, you are the one who crosses the ocean of existence; by relying upon you, the wise have reached the further shore through spiritual practice alone. (259)
Because the fruit of the infinite meritorious deeds performed in previous lives has arisen today, I am present here; therefore, I am a vessel for your compassion. (260)
Beholding a knower of Brahman instantly produces delight for the eyes, serenity of the face, and joy within the heart; it cuts away delusion and reveals the auspicious state.
Even a hundred million fires or moons are unable to destroy that internal delusion which is infinite;
yet the knower of the Self destroys it with a single glance.

In this terrible ocean of existence, difficult to cross, fierce with the intense sufferings of birth, death, and disease, and terrifying with its many crocodiles in the form of sons, wives, and friends; being repeatedly dragged by the mass of high waves and breaking surges of karma, I wander in a cycle of coming and going, yet through my delusion, I see no refuge whatsoever. (263)
By what residue of merit have I beheld your two lotus-feet? Protect me, who am afflicted by death, with your compassionate gaze. (264)
When the disciple speaks thus, the Guru, looking upon him with compassion, should grant him fearlessness, saying repeatedly, "Do not fear. (265)
O wise one, abandon the fear of death; for you, who are eternal, devoid of duality, and whose nature is the Supreme Bliss of Brahman, there is no death whatsoever.
Out of delusion, having perceived something [unreal], you speak falsely with a terrified mind, crying out "Save me!"—this is but empty prattle, like that of one asleep, and is utterly vain.

A person, shrouded in the deep darkness of sleep, perceives in a dream that he has been seized by a serpent or the like and cries out in terror, "I am killed! But when awakened by a trusted friend who strikes him with the palm of his hand and asks him, he himself [realizes the truth].
If he says "nothing at all," tell me: for what purpose would that statement of his exist? (267)

This man, failing to discern the true nature of the rope and grasping it as a snake, cries out "A serpent dwells here! and, out of delusion, trembles with fear; yet that is entirely false, for when investigated, no serpent exists there at all. (268)
In the same way, you have also described this suffering of birth, dissolution, disease, old age, and so forth as belonging to the self;
all of it is indeed false, imagined through delusion. Having investigated thoroughly within yourself, abandon your fear.
You grieve by superimposing the non-self phenomena upon the self;
abandon all that fear caused by ignorance and become happy. (270)
The disciple [objects]:
"Everything stated by the venerable ones is false;
for only an example can be logically established."
The suffering of existence and so forth is directly evident even to a commoner, as it is well-known to all people. ||271||
How can an object experienced through direct perception deserve to be false?
How could I make a jar, which is the object of the eye, false? (272)
O Lord, how can the falsity of that which exists be possible?
For indeed, direct perception is the most evident of all means of valid cognition. (273)
For me, a mortal who partakes in the sufferings of birth and so forth and possesses but a short life, how can there be even the state of Brahman, eternity, or supreme bliss? (274)
What is the self and what is the non-self? What is the defining characteristic of these two? And how is it that the attributes of the non-self are superimposed upon the self? (275)
What is ignorance, and how is there the abandonment of the fear produced by it?
What is knowledge, and how is there the attainment of the bliss produced by it? (276)
O Lord, O Śrī Guru, O ocean of compassion, please cause all of this to be clearly realized by me, as vividly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand, just as before. (277)
The glorious Guru is blessed and his purpose is fulfilled; oh, what discernment you possess!
Great indeed is the grace of Śiva that resides within you.
Since you strive to realize Brahman, having abandoned the path of the worldly realm. ||278||
Without the grace of Śiva there is no accomplishment;
without the grace of Śiva there is no wisdom;
without the grace of Śiva there is no reasoning.
Without the grace of Śiva, there is no liberation. ||279||
By whose grace Śuka and others were freed from attachment and released from the bonds of saṃsāra—
his grace is obtained only after many births.
Accessible through devotion alone, he is the cause of liberation from worldly existence. ||280||
Discernment arises for living beings even amidst many births,
solely through divine grace and by the power of the ripening of abundant past merits;
therefore, you too [should apply yourself] toward the realization of the ultimate truth.
This is the fruit of discernment for men who have undertaken their endeavors in this world. ||281||

They declare that liberation is indeed the primary fruit for the attainment of mortality, the attainment of manhood, the attainment of Brahminhood, and the attainment of discernment; for if liberation does not exist, all of these would be in vain. (282)
This question of yours is most excellent, in that you are engaged in the realization of the true nature of the self;
therefore, all this [of yours] shall be uprooted.
I shall announce it with joy; listen! ||283||
Mortality has been imagined in you through the power of delusion; from that very [delusion] comes birth, and consequently, the suffering associated with it. Yet, in reality, that is false for you.
Is the pleasure or the pain experienced under the influence of sleep and delusion anything real to you?
Tell me, in the dawn of awakening, has anything ever been perceived as being real? (284)
One should not suspect that this entire phenomenal world, which is being experienced directly by all people without exception,
could be false.
By you, who are devoid of discernment and utterly deluded. ||285||
Is the darkness perceived by one blind during the day— though established by direct perception— ever real? In the same way, is an object understood through delusion [ever real]?
It is real for one who is deluded, but merely false for one of sound intelligence. ||286||
In the cognition "this is a jar," some verbal designation of a jar arises from perception;
yet, when investigated, that [designation] does not exist therein.
That clay is distinct from its state of being [as a jar].
The sun is perceived as being only a span in size,
yet by scripture it is shown to be eighty-four thousand yojanas; thus,
in some cases, one measurement is sublated by another.
For even in this case, there is no established certainty regarding direct perception.
Therefore, know that this which appears to you as wandering is indeed false and not real;
you yourself are directly Brahman, whose very nature is bliss.
Discern that it is not distinct from you within your own intellect.
Neither in another world, nor here in a cave, nor at another sacred ford, nor within the succession of karma,
nor in another scripture— none of these do we perceive here.
When the supreme Brahman itself is being investigated. ||290||
Not knowing the reality that resides within himself, the fool looks for it in the scriptures, like a dull-witted cowherd searching for a goat already in his armpit while looking into wells. (291)
Thinking one's own self to be another and the Supreme Self to be otherwise, the wise search for their own self once again outside in various sheaths. (292)
Having forgotten the true nature of the object and having superimposed [falsity] upon it, one vainly grieves over its non-existence and its properties; it is not otherwise. //293//
I shall explain to you the discrimination between the Self and the non-Self; listen with reverence, for by the mere hearing of it, one is liberated from the bondage of the non-Self. (294)
Having spoken thus and having turned his disciple toward him with compassion, the Guru,
by means of superimposition and negation, unfolds that which is free from conceptual proliferation.
He correctly awakened to reality by way of the path seen in the scriptures;
for the benefit of all, that method is shown here. (296)
||13 ||Superimposition (adhyāropa) ||

The superimposition of a non-entity upon an entity is called *adhyāropa*, just as, for example, the superimposition of the nature of a snake upon a rope or similar object that is not actually a snake. (297)
The reality is, first of all, the Supreme Brahman, characterized by truth, knowledge, and so forth;
that upon which this superimposed world shines, like the blueness and other qualities in the sky. (298)
That ignorance, along with its effects, which is distinct from reality and whose sublation is observed, is called "non-existent" by the wise. (299)
That which is sublated by means of valid cognitions is non-existent, like silver in a mother-of-pearl shell;
that which is not sublated is an existent entity throughout the three times, like the mother-of-pearl shell itself. (300)

Just as there is indeed no sublation of the mother-of-pearl when it is [mistaken for] silver, so too that which is designated as "non-existent" is the cause of the superimposition of this world. (301)

Ignorance is indefinable as either being or non-being; it consists of the three *guṇas*, is a real entity, is to be sublated solely by the awakening to reality, and is characterized by its very existence. (302)
There, it remains based upon Brahman through a false connection;
just as the power [of a gem] resides in the gem, so too this [ignorance] does not corrupt its substratum. ||303||
The evidence for its existence is this: the entire world of moving and non-moving beings is its effect;
the authority consists of the Śruti, the Smṛti, and even the personal experience of "I am ignorant. (304)
Ignorance is called *prakṛti*, power (*śakti*), and *avidyā*;
this is neither existent nor non-existent, like silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. (305)
Whether distinct or non-distinct from the existent, it is not like the light of a lamp;
nor is it ever possessed of parts or otherwise, like the sprout of a seed. (306)
Therefore, the wise know this very thing to be inexpressible; ignorance is said to be twofold, by way of both the collective and the individual. (307)
Through the non-differentiation of various cognitions perceived as distinct,
there arises a unity as a collective whole, just as a forest is formed by trees.
This supreme totality, which from of old has been characterized solely by pure *sattva* due to the excellence of its *sattva*-component, is called *māyā* by those who know it. (309)
Ishvara: ||14||

Consciousness conditioned by Māyā, accompanied by the light of the intellect, augmented by the quality of Sattva, and endowed with attributes such as omniscience, is the cause of creation, maintenance, and dissolution. ||310||
That which is unmanifest is called the Indeterminate (avyākṛta) and is also sung of as the Lord (īśa);
it is endowed with all powers and qualities, and is the illuminator of all knowledge. ||311||
He is the independent Lord, whose will is true and whose desires are true;
he is this Great Viṣṇu, the possessor of great power and supreme majesty. ||312||
Because it is the cause of omniscience, lordship, and so forth, the wise call the body—the collective whole augmented by *sattva*—the "cause" (*kāraṇa*). (313)
Because it abounds in bliss and because it is the means of realization, like a sheath,
this very one is declared to be the "sheath consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya-kośa) of the Lord.

Because it is the cause of the cessation of everything, it is held to be the state of deep sleep; it is there that the primordial dissolution (prākṛta-pralaya) is repeatedly proclaimed by the Vedas. //315//
Ignorance appears as manifold due to the perspective of individual distinctions; the various functions of ignorance are distinct according to their respective qualities. (316)
Just as the multiplicity of "trees" arises from the perspective of the individuality of the forest, so too does multiplicity arise from the individuality of ignorance. (317)
O inner self!
This individual manifestation (vyaṣṭi) consists of impure being (sattva) joined with passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas);
therefore, it is inferior and serves as the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the inner self (pratyagātman). ||318||
Consciousness, when delimited by the individual (vyaṣṭi), is celebrated as the inner self (pratyagātman);
accompanied by the light [of consciousness] and conditioned by the individual, it appears through identity with existence and its qualities. ||319||

That very Self, when overcome [by limitations], is designated as the "living being" (jīva); it possesses such attributes as limited knowledge, lack of sovereignty, and the state of being subject to transmigratory existence. //320//

Its individual manifestation is the cause by virtue of being the cause of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra); the self that identifies with the body therein is called "the wise one" (prājña) by the learned. (321)
Its status as "the wise" is accepted on the grounds that it illuminates a single ignorance;
because the individual soul (vyaṣṭi) is inferior, it does not illuminate multiple ignorances. ||322||
Because it veils one's true nature and because it abounds in bliss, the causal body is called the "sheath consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya-kośa). ||323||
This state is deep sleep (suṣupti), wherein bliss is fully manifested; [one reflects]: "I slept happily, yet I was not conscious of anything. (325)
In reality, there is no difference between us because of the oneness of our genus;
thus, non-difference alone is to be understood even in the case of the Lord and the individual soul. (326)
If the substrate and the attribute are non-different, where is the difference between those two as qualified by them?
When there is oneness, what difference is there between the wave and the ocean, or between two reflections? (327)
That pure consciousness which is the substratum for both ignorance and its delimited reflection is called the Fourth (turya). ||328||

This very same [reality], when not yet distinguished from the limiting adjuncts and their qualities, is the expressed meaning (vācyārtha) of the Great Sentence; when distinguished, it is held to be the indicated meaning (lakṣya). ||329||
16 || Īśvara:
The Lord, endowed with infinite power and having Māyā as His limiting adjunct,
creates this entire universe of moving and non-moving beings by mere glance.
This Lord, who is without a second and consists solely of Himself, is without any material cause;
therefore, one should not doubt how He creates everything by Himself alone. (331)
The Lord himself, being both the efficient cause (nimitta) and the material cause (upādāna),
creates, sustains, and dissolves the universe consisting of the moving and the unmoving.
By virtue of its own primacy, it is the efficient cause (nimitta-kāraṇa) of the world; therefore, by virtue of the primacy of its adjuncts (upādhi), it becomes the material cause (upādāna). //333//
17. The creation of the five elements.
Just as a spider and its web exist through its own predominance, so too does the Lord exist through the predominance of his own body. (334)
From the Supreme Self, which is characterized by primordial nature (prakṛti) dominated by the quality of darkness (tamas), space (ākāśa) arose; from space, wind (vāyu) is said to have arisen. (335)
From wind comes fire, from fire water, and from water earth, in succession;
the predominance of tamas in śakti is evident from the observation of inertia in its effects. (336)
For those qualities of the effect indeed originate from the qualities of the cause;
these subtle elements (sūkṣmabhūta) are likewise the mere constituents of the gross elements (bhūtamātra), arising in due order.
The subtle body.
From these subtle elements, subtle bodies also arise;
likewise, gross elements come into being through the mutual blending of their parts. (338)
Born from the unquintuplicated elements, consisting of seventeen components, the subtle body (liṅga) is the cause of transmigratory existence and the instrument for the self's experience. (339)
The pentad of the ear and so forth, the pentad of speech and so forth, the pentad of the vital breath and so forth, along with the intellect and the mind, are called the subtle body (liṅga). ||340||
The five—ear, speech, eye, tongue, and nose—were born; from the sentient portions of space and the other elements, the faculties of cognition arose in succession. (341)
The internal organ.
The five sattvic portions residing in space and the other elements, having merged together, became the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), which is the cause of everything.
Because these [faculties] possess the quality of illumination, they are held to consist of the *sāttvika* portion;
for illumination belongs to *sattva* by virtue of its transparency. (343)
That internal organ, through its different functions, is fourfold;
it is called the mind (manas), the intellect (buddhi), the ego (ahaṅkāra), and the consciousness (citta). ||344||
They call the mind (manas) "volition" (saṃkalpa), the intellect (buddhi) from its determination of an object;
the ego (ahaṅkāra) from its self-conceit, and the heart (citta) from its reflection upon an object. (345)

Furthermore, it should be understood that *manas* and *buddhi*, as well as *citta* and *ahaṃkāra*, are included here respectively for the sake of establishing the definition of the subtle body (*liṅga*). (346)
Just as reflection, volition, and so forth are attributes of the mind, so too the inclusion of the *samyakcitta* (right thought) within the mind itself is established. 347.

Because the notion "I" with respect to the body and so forth is observed to be extremely firm in the intellect, it is therefore logical that the inclusion of egoism (ahaṅkāra) occurs here [within the buddhi]. ||348||
Therefore, the agency belongs to the intellect alone, while that which is other than it possesses the nature of an instrument;
one should understand that for the Self, both arise from delusion, which is the cause of saṃsāra. (349)
The sheath consisting of consciousness (vijñānamaya-kośa).
The sheath consisting of consciousness (vijñānamaya-kośa) consists of the intellect together with the organs of knowledge;
it is so called because of its abundance of consciousness and because it veils the Self. ||350||
This is called the "sheath consisting of consciousness" by the wise;
it is the Great One, characterized as the agent, possessing the function of egoism. (351)
This very person, possessing the conceit of being a living soul, always maintains the egoistic notions of "I" and "mine" with respect to the body, the senses, the home, and so forth.
The agent, the enjoyer, the happy one, and the suffering one. ||352||
Impelled solely by one's own latent predispositions, one constantly performs actions characterized by both [virtue and non-virtue],
and experiences the specific results produced thereby.
Both happiness and suffering, both here and in the next world. ||353||
Being born again and again in thousands of diverse wombs and dying repeatedly, this living soul wanders within the circle of saṃsāra. (354)
The sheath consisting of mind.
The sheath made of mind (manomaya-kośa) consists of the mind together with the organs of cognition;
that in which the predominance of the mind is observed is the "made of mind" (manomaya). ||355||
Thought, despondency, joy, and so forth, as well as desire and the like, are its functions.
It is by means of the mind alone that it thinks; it desires the fruit externally;
it exerts effort, acts, and experiences—thus the mind is the cause of everything. (356)
For the mind is the cause of this inclination; by means of it, one knows the object both internally and externally.
By means of this very [mind], one hears, smells, sees, speaks, touches, eats, and performs every action. (357)
Bondage and liberation for men are achieved by the mind alone; likewise, both what is beneficial and what is harmful are accomplished by this very same [mind].
Through purity comes liberation, through impurity bondage; through discernment comes what is beneficial, and through lack of discernment, the opposite. (358)

Stained by *rajas* and *tamas*, impure, born of ignorance, and devoid of the quality of *sattva*, the mind—due to its being possessed by the defects of *tamas*—is characterized by dullness, delusion, sloth, and negligence; thus, being obscured, it does not perceive the true reality of objects even when they are being apprehended. (359)
If it is joined with the defects of passion (rajas), constantly overwhelmed by the opposing qualities such as desire and the like, it causes distress;
even if it somehow possesses an understanding of subtle objects, it wanders greatly astray.
Just as the lamp of the mind has its power destroyed by a violent wind.
Then, the seeker of liberation, for the sake of release from the bondage of worldly existence,
having separated the mind from rajas and tamas along with their effects, [makes it] composed of pure sattva.
One should always act with effort to do what is pleasing. ||361||
Having repeatedly contemplated the suffering seen among living beings in the womb, birth, destruction, old age, disease, and so forth, as well as that which exists in hell;

and having observed only the defects in all sense objects, let the wise person completely release their attachment and firmly take hold of spiritual strength in order to untie the knots of the mind. (362)
The mind of one who is devoted to the restraints (yama) and diligently applies himself to the observances (niyama) attains clarity through discernment. ||363||
Having abandoned the demonic endowment, he who constantly resorts to the divine endowment with the sole desire for liberation, his mind becomes serene. (364)
The mind of one whose thoughts do not dwell upon the wealth of others, the injury of others, the censuring of others, or the wives of others becomes serene. (365)
He who perceives all beings with equanimity as his own self, and distinguishes between pleasure and pain, his mind becomes serene. (366)
The mind of one who, being patient, constantly worships the Guru as the Lord within oneself with extreme faith and devotion, becomes serene. (367)
The eating of remnants, worship of the Lord, service to the noble, pilgrimage to sacred fords, steadfastness in the duties of one’s own stage of life,
adherence to the restraints (yamas), and persistence in the observances (niyamas).
Those who know the truth speak thus for the sake of clarifying the mind. ||368||
The abandonment of pungent, sour, salty, excessively hot, sharp, and dry foods, as well as putrid and stale food and the like, conduces to the welfare of sentient beings. (369)
Through hearing the Purāṇas of the nature of goodness, through service to things of the nature of goodness, and through following the virtuous, the conduct of goodness arises. (370)
He whose mind is free from objects and whose heart is cool—his entire world is a friend, and liberation is held in the palm of his hand. (371)
One who eats wholesome food in moderation, always resorts to solitude,

speaks what is appropriate and beneficial only once, sleeps and amuses himself sparingly, and is disciplined in following instructions— whoever practices this at the prescribed times, [attains success].
He quickly attains here a virtuous clarity of mind. ||372||
Without clarity of mind, one cannot understand the reality of the self and the other;
yet without the realization of that reality, liberation is not achieved, even through ten million billion Brahmas. (373)
Mental heedlessness is the bondage of a person; mental clarity is liberation from the bond of worldly existence.
Therefore, for the sake of attaining mental clarity, the wise man should effect the withdrawal of the mind. (374)
The sheath consisting of vital breath (prāṇamaya-kośa).
From the portions of *rajas* of these very five elements, there arose in sequence the organs of action:
speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the genitals. (375)
From all the portions of *rajas*, the five internal winds—prāṇa and the others—which are of the nature of activity, have arisen from space and the other elements. (376)
Prāṇa exists by moving forward, and apāna by moving downward;
vyāna is so called because of its movement in all directions, while udāna is intended [to be known] by its upward departure.
The wind which is the fifth among those [winds] is intended as the "equalizing" (samāna) because of its nature of equalizing the food, juices, and so forth that have been consumed. //378//
Action alone is generally assigned to the vital breaths and the organs of action;
therefore, the wise have accepted that the birth of these [organs] is from the portions of *rajas*. (379)
The great seers have declared that the rajasic power is the power of action, the tamasic power is of an insentient nature, and the sattvic power is of the nature of light. ||380||
