These five, beginning with prāṇa, together with the five organs of action, constitute the sheath consisting of vital breath (prāṇamaya-kośa), by which the gross body is set in motion. (381)
Whatever action is performed— whether meritorious or indeed sinful—
by means of speech and so forth, or by the body, it has as its agent that which consists of vital breath (prāṇamaya).
Just as a tree shaken by the wind moves in various ways, yet when that [wind] is stilled, it too becomes still; so it is in this case.
The body, impelled by the vital breaths and the organs of action, engages in various activities everywhere, whether prescribed or prohibited. (384)
When these three sheaths are combined, this becomes the subtle body of the self;
for it serves as the means of perceiving the self that is merged in extreme subtlety.
That which is subtle is considered the "liṅga" (the mark) in relation to the gross;
everything is born with the body of a liṅga because it is the object of a single cognition. (386)
Just as a multitude of trees constitutes a forest by way of their collective totality (sāmānya),
so too they declare that consciousness conditioned by this collective totality is the "fruitful" one.
The wise also call him Hiraṇyagarbha, Sūtrātman, and Prāṇa;
he shines like gold within the golden womb of the intellect. (388)
Therefore, the designation "Hiraṇyagarbha" is recognized for him.

Because he exists pervading all subtle bodies (liṅgadehas) like a thread through a string of jewels, he is called the "Sūtrātman"; and because he causes the vitalizing function (prāṇana), he is called "Prāṇa. (389)
Furthermore, the individual (vyaṣṭi) does not become a logical mark (liṅga) by virtue of being an object of multiple cognitions;
rather, it is that which is conditioned by the individual and endowed with the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa). ||390||
The wise declare that consciousness is *taijasa* (the radiant);
it is called *taijasa* precisely because it is conditioned by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) which consists of light. //391//

Its individual manifestation (*vyaṣṭi*) is considered to be its subtle body (*sūkṣmavapuḥ*), because it is subtler than the gross [body]; it is called a "body" (*vapuḥ*) because it consists of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the waking state. (392)
In the dream state, the Taijasa self enjoys objects fashioned by the latent impressions (vāsanā) of the waking state—subtle objects through subtle mental functions. ||393||

Furthermore, just as before, the non-difference alone is to be understood between the aggregate and the individual by way of their commonality; for when there is oneness of genus, how could there be any distinction? (394)
When two limiting adjuncts (upādhi) are one, their respective presiding deities are also non-different;
thus, as before, the non-difference of the mind (manas) and the taijasa [deity] is held to follow from the Sūtra.
Thus has the classification of the subtle phenomenal world been described according to the scriptures. Now, the classification of the gross phenomenal world is being told; listen. (396)
Those very subtle elements, beginning with space, become gross through mutual quintuplication; hear now the sequence of that process. (397)
Each of the elements [of the body] is divided equally into two parts;
having thus divided them, one should discard the first portion and take the second portion. (398)

Then, having divided that [circle] into four equal parts, one should place each [of the remaining elements] in the first quarter of each of the four [sections], at intervals of half its own size in sequence.
From that, there are five parts of the elements beginning with space;
four of those parts are obtained from the others by means of their own respective half-parts. (400)

By being combined, ether and the other elements attain grossness in their respective order; one should not suspect that this process of quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa) lacks authoritative validity. 401.
The scriptural passage concerning the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) is merely an illustration;
elsewhere, the origin of all five elements is also heard. (402)
Therefore, let the wise consider the fivefold division (pañcīkaraṇa) to be authoritative;
otherwise, if it were done differently, there would be contradiction with perception and other means of valid cognition. (403)
Space, wind, and dharma are perceived in fire and so forth;
however, space and wind are not observed as properties of fire and the like in that same manner. (404)
Therefore, let nothing that lacks a valid basis be considered;
for the pervasion of its own parts and the pervasion of space exist in fire and other such things. (405)
Therefore, sound is perceived as distinct from its cause;
likewise, the property of air is also perceived in fire and other such phenomena. (406)
In that same way, pervasion by fire and so forth does not exist in the case of space and the wind;
because of their subtlety, due to the pervasion of their constituent parts, that property is not perceived. (407)
Everywhere the effect is seen to correspond to its cause;
therefore, the wise should accept the validity [of the Veda] even on account of its being composed of the five elements.
||23 ||The Fivefold Process (Pañcīkaraṇa) ||
By this, I shall state the true nature of the elements along with their emergent qualities; listen attentively:
space has sound as its sole quality, while wind possesses the qualities of sound and touch. (409)
Fire is the cause possessing the qualities of sound, touch, and form in sequence;
water possesses four qualities: sound, touch, form, and taste, in sequence. (410)
Together with these four, the earth possesses five qualities;
through its portion of space, the ear perceives sound, which is its specific quality. (411)
The skin, being a portion of air, perceives touch as its quality;
the eye, being a portion of fire, perceives form as its quality. ||412||
The tongue perceives taste through its watery component, which possesses that quality;
the nose perceives smell through its earthy component, which possesses that quality. (413)
By means of its vocal component, it performs the activity of uttering words;
by means of its aerial component, the two feet are intent upon activities such as walking. (414)
The hands, being portions of fire, are intent upon the worship of Agni and other deities;
the organ of generation, being a portion of water, effects the discharge of semen and urine. (415)
The anus, by virtue of its share of the earth element, should discharge solid waste;
the deity of the ear is the quarters of space, while wind is the deity of the skin and the sun is that of the eyes. 416.
The deities of the sense faculties.
Varuṇa is the deity of the tongue, both Aśvins of the sense of smell;
Agni is the deity of speech, Indra of the two hands, and Trivikrama of the feet. ||417||
Death is the presiding deity of speech; Prajāpati is the presiding deity of the generative organ with respect to the divine.
The Moon is the deity of the mind, and Bṛhaspati is the deity of the intellect. ||418||

Rudra is the deity of the ego (ahaṃkāra), while the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is the deity of the mind (citta). All the deities beginning with the directions are born from the sattva-portion of the elements starting with space (ākāśa).
Proportionate to the locations of the sense-faculties, they restrain and assist the faculties from all sides, in accordance with the karma of living beings.
The body, the collection of instruments, the vital breaths, the ego, and the presiding deities—these five are declared to be the causes for the accomplishment of all actions. (421)
In accordance with karma, there arises the emergence of qualities; in accordance with qualities, the mind functions.
Through the senses, which consist of both [aspects] and follow the lead of the mind, merit and demerit are produced here.
The one consisting of consciousness, abiding as that very self, conceives the conceit, "I alone am the doer";
but the Self is the witness, it does nothing at all, nor does it cause anything to be done, remaining forever like a bystander.
The ego (ahaṅkāra) becomes the seer, the hearer, the speaker, the doer, and the enjoyer;
the Self (ātman), however, is itself the witness of these transformations and is entirely untainted.
The Self possesses only the state of being a witness; it has neither agency nor the status of an enjoyer, like the sun among the actions performed by living beings in the world. (425)
For the sun performs no action, nor does it cause living beings to act;
they proceed in their respective activities in accordance with their own inherent natures. 426.
In the very same way, the inner self (pratyagātman), like the sun, remains indifferent through its inactive nature amidst the activities of the body and other such factors. ||427||
Not knowing this supreme reality, those whose minds are deluded by māyā superimpose upon their own selves such things as agency, which belong to other domains. (428)

Without investigating the true nature of the Self, the deluded intellect superimposes all these non-self effects upon it—just as, through error, one perceives the movement caused by distant clouds upon the moon, which is itself detached consciousness and actionless within its own being. (429)
25. The Origin of the World.
We shall explain the discrimination between the Self and the non-Self more clearly further on.
O learned one, listen now to this manner of the world's origin through its cyclic recurrence. (430)
From the elements such as ether and the rest, which have been quintuplicated, this gross cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), containing all things moving and stationary, has arisen by the will of the Lord. 431.
All plants such as rice, as well as wind, fire, water, and earth—these became the food for all four classes of embodied beings. (432)
Some indeed subsist on air, while others consume the radiance of the moon and sun;
some, innumerable, feed on drops of water, while others eat earth;
some are intent on eating leaves, stones, and grass, while others are meat-eaters.
Some of these living beings subsist by being devoted to eating food made of rice and barley. ||433||
The fourfold collection of living beings.
Beings born from a womb, from an egg, from sweat, and from sprouting—these four types of creatures remain as they have arisen, in accordance with their respective karmas. (434)
Those humans and others who are born from wombs are "womb-born" (jarāyuja);
those birds and others who are born from eggs are "egg-born" (aṇḍaja). ||435||
Those born from sweat are "sweat-born" (svedaja), such as lice, nits, and the like;
those born by breaking through the earth are "earth-born" (udbhijja), such as trees and the like. (436)
This [universe], which has arisen as a gross body and consists of the fourfold elements, is generally a collective whole (*samaṣṭi*) because it is the object of a single cognition. (437)
The Vedists declare that this consciousness, delimited by the aggregate [of the elements] and conjoined with its fruit, is called Vaiśvānara and Virāj. (438)
Vaiśvānara is so called because of the identification [of him] as the Self within all men;
he is the Virāj because of his manifold nature, shining forth by himself. (439)
The fourfold collection of elements, according to their respective specific types,
is not accepted as a distinct individual (vyaṣṭi) in the same manner as before, because they do not constitute a single object of cognition.

Those proficient in the Vedānta system say that consciousness, together with its appearance, conditioned by the individual (vyaṣṭi), and having attained identity with that [individual], is the universe. ||441||
Because this Viśva exists here within this gross body through self-identification, it therefore possesses its name "Viśva" in accordance with its meaning. 442.
This is the individual manifestation of this universe, possessing a gross body;
because it is a transformation of food, it is called the "sheath composed of food" (annamaya-kośa).
This body is born from the transformation of the food consumed by the parents, namely semen and blood;
it grows through food and perishes in its absence. (444)
Therefore, because it is a transformation of food, this [body] is considered "consisting of food" (annamaya);
and because it covers the self, like the sheath of a sword, it is also so called. (445)
They know this to be the abode of the gross enjoyments of the self;
situated within the gross self, it experiences gross objects such as sound and the rest. (446)
Therefore, the external self is called the locus for gross enjoyment.
The wise say that this [self], joined with the body, senses, and mind, is itself the enjoyer of sounds and other objects presented by the senses. (447)

In this body, which possesses eleven gates like a palace, this Self—served by the group of senses as if by a great king—remained established in the subtle body (upādi) and enjoyed the experiences of sense objects. 448.
The organs of perception, impelled by their respective presiding deities, as well as the organs of action and the mind and so forth,
remain fixed in the performance of their own specific functions.
They attend upon him with effort, like servants. ||449||
When this one of great intelligence experiences gross objects [of sense], characterized by the notions of "I" and "mine," that state of his is called the waking state. (450)

The non-difference between that [totality] and Viśva-Vaiśvānara, as well as between their respective presiding deities, is held to be as previously stated for both the collective and the individual. (451)
Whatever manifestations have been described—termed gross, subtle, and causal—all of them together constitute one great manifestation. ||452||

That consciousness alone is one and the same, though it appears divided by the great proliferation (mahāprapañca) and is characterized as Viśva, Prājña, and so forth, extending from Virāṭ up to Īśvara. ||453||
That which is without beginning or end, unmanifest, consciousness, unborn, and imperishable, exists like fire, undifferentiated from the great phenomenal world.
The learned have determined that for the statement "All this, indeed, is Brahman," there is both an expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*) and a distinct indicated meaning (*lakṣya*). (455)
O wise one, understand that everything which is visible—from the gross [body] up to the ignorance of the unmanifest—is characterized by cause and effect, and is therefore not the Self. 456.
||27 ||The Self||
With a subtle intellect, understand that the Self is that consciousness which is the witness of the internal organ and its modifications, eternal and changeless. (457)
This [Self] is self-luminous through direct perception, partless, unattached, pure, and always of a single nature;
it is of the form of eternal, indivisible bliss, effortless, the witness, consciousness, absolute, and devoid of qualities. 458.
The Self is never born, nor does it grow;
it neither diminishes nor undergoes destruction.
This Self is eternal, everlasting, and ancient.
He is not slain when the body is being slain.
Birth, existence, growth, transformation, decay, and destruction— these six modifications of the perceptible alone constitute various diseases;
likewise, grossness and so forth, blueness and so forth, as well as the manifestation of color, smell, and other qualities, are all merely measurements of that which is perceived.
These [faculties] are seen as witnesses to the modifications of that [body], yet they do not belong to the body nor to the self. ||460||
Having superimposed the nature of non-self upon this self, and conversely the nature of self upon that which is not the self, people wander through cyclic existence due to delusion. (461)

"Through delusion, they falsely imagine within the Self: 'I am a human,' 'I am a twice-born,' 'I am a knower,' 'I am ignorant,' 'I am exceedingly sinful,' 'I am fallen,' 'I am refined,' 'I am happy,' or 'I am miserable. (462)

Due to the defect of their intellect, they erroneously superimpose upon this [self], which is not of such a nature, the qualities of birth, old age, death, hunger, thirst, pleasure, affliction, fear, and so forth, which belong to what is non-self. (463)
Wherever there is a superimposition of something due to delusion, that [substratum] is never connected with even the slightest quality or defect produced by that [superimposed thing]. (464)
Does the wind become wet by the flood of water in a mirage? Or does a conch shell turn yellow simply because it is perceived as yellow by the eye? (465)
Does the sky become darkened by the blueness imagined by the wind?
O Lord, how can there be the superimposition of the non-self upon the inner Self, which is not an object of cognition? 466.
For when an object is perceived before one, another object is superimposed upon it;
this is observed in the case of mother-of-pearl, a rope, and so forth, due to the connection with similarity and other factors. (467)

Superimposition is the appearance elsewhere of something previously perceived, characterized by memory; O Lord, how could that occur with respect to the Self, which is beyond the range of the senses? (468)
The self has never been experienced; how can there be a similarity established for an object that has not been experienced, when it is of a different nature from the non-self? (469)
How has this superimposition of the self upon the non-self come about? How is its cessation achieved, and by what means is it accomplished? (470)
The connection with limiting adjuncts (upādhi) is exactly the same for both the Lord and the individual soul;
why then is bondage only for the soul and not for the Lord? How can that be so? (471)
O omniscient Śrī Guru, ocean of compassion, please explain all of this clearly through your merciful gaze, as plainly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand. 472.
The venerable Guru [says]:
"The Self is not held to be composed of parts, nor is it an object; for it is the referent of the notion 'I' and is entirely immediate. (473)
The self is indeed well-established, yet it is not perceived by anyone;
for there is no cognition such as "I do not exist" regarding the inner self.
No means of valid cognition is required for the own-existence of anything;
rather, what establishes the validity of the means of valid cognition themselves is that which brings about awareness. (475)

This Self is not experienced when obscured by the effects of illusion (māyā), just as the sun is [not seen] by masses of clouds; so too is this [Self obscured] by the "I" and other such [notions]. (476)
The wise have not established a rule that superimposition must occur only with respect to an object situated in front; rather, error itself is the cause in this matter. //477//

Just as the wise superimpose blueness and other qualities upon the sky, which is not an object of sight or other senses, so too do they [superimpose them] upon this Self due to a delusion of the intellect. //478//
In the superimposition of selfhood upon what is not-self, similarity is not required;
for in cases such as "this conch is yellow," what need is there for similarity? (479)
In this regard, dependence is observed only in errors that are without limiting adjuncts (nirupādhi);
it is seen only in those with limiting adjuncts (sopādhi), such as the error of a rope-snake and the like. ||480||
Nevertheless, I shall say something; listen with focused attention to that similarity:
this self is utterly pure, subtle, and exceedingly luminous. (481)
In the same way, the self of sentient beings is luminous and stainless, yet it appears as if possessed of a self due to proximity [to the ego], just as a crystal appears like the sun. (482)
From that, the intellect (buddhi) appears as the self; from that, the mind (manas) appears as the intellect;
the sense organs appear as the mind; and this body appears as the sense organs.
For this very reason, there arises the notion of "self" with respect to the body and the senses, which are not the self.
Just as a reflection and so forth appear to the deluded, even as they do to children, a semblance exists in the intellect which serves as the cause for the superimposition of the self. ||484||
This superimposition which has been described as "I" in what is not the self—this preceding superimposition is indeed the cause for each subsequent superimposition. (485)
The characteristic of transmigratory existence is observed precisely in those who have awakened from sleep or fainting;
this beginningless [state] arises from ignorance, and the mental impression (saṃskāra) is likewise of that same nature.
Listen with a concentrated mind as I shall explain the cause for the arrival of this sublation of superimposition,
from which this collection of misfortunes has arisen.
Birth, death, disease, old age, and other such sufferings. ||487||

Ignorance, which is the limiting adjunct of the self, possesses two great powers: projection and concealment; by means of these two, the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra) occurs for the self. (488)
The power of darkness is obscuration; it is the cause of veiling.
It is called "root ignorance" (mūlāvidyā), by which the world is deluded. (489)

Even one who possesses discernment, even one who is highly rational, even one who has heard the truth of the Self, and even one who is learned—if by a certain power his vision of awakening is obscured, he does not know this Self abiding within himself. (490)

The power of *rajas*, named "distraction," is the eternal cause of activity for the *puruṣa*; by it, this entire universe—from the gross elements down to the subtle *liṅga*—though non-existent in the Self, is constantly brought forth as if it were real. (491)
Just as sleep envelops even a vigilant man,
so too does this power of obscuration (āvṛti-śakti) envelop the power of internal distraction (vikṣepa-śakti), causing it to expand.

When the true nature of reality is completely shrouded by the powerful veil known as *āvaraṇa*, the person, through delusion, conceives the notion of selfhood, thinking "I am this very [unreal] non-self. (493)

Just as one has the notion of selfhood toward the body that appears in deep sleep, so too does one superimpose upon the Self—which is not the Self—the birth, destruction, hunger, fear, fragmentation, fatigue, and other attributes belonging to that [body]. (494)
Impelled by the power of distraction,
it performs actions of both natures;
and experiencing the fruit thus acquired, it continues to do so.
He indeed wanders about in the ocean of existence. ||495||
This powerful bondage of saṃsāra has come upon the inner self due to the defect of superimposition;
through its connection, one is tormented incessantly by the fears of the afflictions of dwelling in the womb, birth, and death. (496)
Superimposition (adhyāsa) is indeed the apprehension of one thing as another;
it is rooted in natural delusion and is the primal cause of transmigratory existence. (497)
The seed of all misfortune is that misconception regarding the self;
from that follows the descent into saṃsāra, characterized by continuous affliction. (498)
Samsara exists only because of superimposition; when superimposition is destroyed, it is no longer seen.
Therefore, observe clearly both of these states in those who are bound and those who are liberated. (499)
Know that one is bound through engagement and know that one is liberated through withdrawal;
engagement itself is saṃsāra, while withdrawal is held to be liberation. (500)
This superimposition upon the Self is preceded by false knowledge;
though it is unreal, it extends the cycle of worldly existence, like a snake [projected] upon a rope. (501)

Even though the connection with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is equal for both, the Supreme Self does not undergo bondage like the individual soul (*jīva*), nor does it possess any of its effects, due to the difference in those adjuncts. (502)
Its limiting adjunct (upādhi) is Māyā, in which pure Sattva predominates; for in that state, there is not even a trace of its limited nature. Bondage arises from the preeminence of Sattva alone.
There is not even a trace of distraction caused by that. ||503||
The Lord himself, omniscient and possessing the power of unimpeded consciousness, having relied upon his own *māyā*, is the Sovereign whose activity is autonomous due to his immovability;
by the mere will for the operations of creation, maintenance, consumption, entry, and restraint, he acts.
While performing [these], he sports, having suppressed both that rajas and tamas by means of your power.
Therefore, obscuration and distraction are unable to do anything at all;
for he is himself independent in both the engagement in and the cessation of those two. (505)
The Śruti declares that very [power] to be the cognitive activity of the Great Lord, since his power consists in restraint and favor, as well as in concealment and projection. (506)
Due to the decline of *sattva*, there is an increase in *rajas* and *tamas*;
likewise, within the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the individual soul (*jīva*), its effects become more powerful. (507)
By that [ignorance], this bondage of the individual soul and its transmigratory existence (saṃsāra) are produced;
therein it constantly encounters suffering and perceives it ever more intensely. (508)
The cause of this cycle of transmigration is superimposition (adhyāsa), which is the misapprehension of objects;
they say that ignorance (ajñāna), characterized by concealment, is the root of superimposition. (509)
28. Cessation of Ignorance.
The cessation of ignorance occurs through knowledge alone, not through action;
for action, being non-contradictory to it, can never be a sublater of ignorance. (510)
A living being is born through karma and perishes through karma alone;
this succession of birth and death is indeed the effect of karma. (511)
There is no other distinct effect produced by this action;
for that action is the product of ignorance, since it increases through ignorance. (512)
That by which something increases cannot bring about its destruction;
for that which coexists with something is not fit for its cessation. (513)
Who indeed is capable of imagining the capacity for destruction in both [knowledge and action], when knowledge always exists in perpetual opposition to all karma? (514)
Therefore, the destruction of ignorance is not accomplished by action alone;
for at the very moment when there is a conjunction with that [action], its progenitor has already been destroyed. (515)
It is logical that only those two things which possess distinct natures are contradictory, just as there is mutual contradiction between darkness and light. (516)
In the same way, both ignorance and knowledge are observed;
the destruction of that [ignorance] cannot be established by anyone without knowledge. (517)
Therefore, for the sake of cutting through ignorance, the wise person should cultivate knowledge;
knowledge is accomplished through the discrimination between the Self and the non-Self, and not otherwise. (518)

Therefore, one whose mind is disciplined must perform the discrimination between the self and the non-self, by which the knot of the notion of "self" regarding what is not the self is torn asunder. (519)
||29 || Refutation of Wrong Views ||520-611||
This debate is set forth for the purpose of discriminating between the self and the non-self, so that the true nature of the self and the non-self may be clearly and distinctly revealed. (520)
Fools who have not heard the Vedānta, yet consider themselves learned;
who are devoid of the grace of the Lord and are averse to the true Guru. (521)
They dispute regarding that point; listen as I shall explain it with due respect:
a certain utterly vulgar person considers his son to be the self. (522)
Because one observes a powerful affection for one's own son as if for oneself, and because [one thinks], "When my son thrives, I thrive; when he perishes, I perish. (523)
Moreover, on the strength of experience, through reasoning, and also from scripture, the Veda declares:
"The self, indeed, has the name 'son'. (524)
Just as one lamp is lit from another, so too is a son born from a father;
for the qualities of the father are observed in the son like a sprout from a seed. (525)
Therefore, this person, being most deluded, thinks that "this son is the self";
another refutes that view, asking: "How can the son be the self? (526)
How can the self be the son merely from affection?
Affection is observed elsewhere as well, toward fields, vessels, wealth, and so forth. (527)
In this body, living beings are held to cherish their affection for a son more than anything else;
even when a house is ablaze, a creature flees, leaving its son behind. (528)
One sells that [body] for the sake of the self and strikes it down when it is disagreeable;
therefore, the son can never truly be one's own self. (529)
A son does not possess the similarity of qualities, form, and so forth that a lamp possesses with its source;
for from one who is free of defects, a defective child may be born, and even from one of excellent qualities, a child of bad character.
All those methods and even all those expressions are mere appearances, like a son's son in a house, regarding all tasks and objects. (531)

In this context, the term "self" (ātman) is applied figuratively to the son in order to indicate lordship; however, according to the primary sense of the Vedic revelation, a son is not called the self.
Therefore, the nature of a self in a son is merely figurative, not primary;
for the referent of the cognition of the word "I" is the body alone, and nothing else.
The conviction "I am the body" is directly perceived by all living beings;
moreover, the Śruti declares that this person consists of the essence of food (annarasamaya).
For his own self indeed speaks of its being a person; therefore, this self is a god—thus has it been determined by the Cārvāka. (535)
Another ordinary person, unable to tolerate that flawed view, [objects]:
"How indeed could the body be the self? For it is dependent and insentient. (536)
Driven by the sense-faculties, this [self] acts nowhere by its own power;
it depends upon the eyes and other faculties, just as householders depend upon their house. (537)
Since the body arises from semen and blood and possesses various states such as infancy and so forth, it is never logically tenable for the body to be the self. (538)
"I am deaf," "I am one-eyed," and "I am mute"—from such experiences, the senses become the Self for those who possess the perception of objects. (539)
That the senses possess consciousness and that the vital breaths (prāṇas) [reside] in the body is established by the Śruti itself in the passage: "They said to Prajāpati, 'Come to this one. (540)
Therefore, another ordinary person, unable to tolerate this, refutes the conclusion that it is logical for the sense faculties to be the self. (541)
How could the sense-faculties be the self? They are instruments, like an axe. For it is never observed that an instrument, such as an axe, possesses consciousness. (542)
In the scriptures, the presiding deities themselves are metaphorically attributed to the sense organs;
however, it is not asserted that the sense organs possess consciousness in a direct sense. (543)
Just as objects are illuminated by insentient things such as lamps, so too is it established for the sense organs, such as the eyes, despite their being insentient. (544)
This vital breath (*prāṇa*), which possesses five functions, is the activator of the sense organs;
it persists through all states and thus assumes the nature of the self (*ātman*), even from such experiences as "I am hungry" or "I am thirsty. (545)

Since another inner self is declared by scripture to be "consisting of breath" (prāṇamaya), it is therefore appropriate that breath constitutes the nature of the Self, and never that of those things designated as instruments (karaṇa). //546//
Another fool refutes this certainty [of his], saying:
"How can the self be the vital breath? This internal breath is simply air. (547)
Moving out and coming in repeatedly like the breath of a bellows, it knows nothing at all—whether beneficial or harmful, its own or another's. (548)
Inert by nature, fickle, and always engaged in activity, the manifestation of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is not perceived when the mind is in a state of sleep. (549)
The mind, however, knows everything and is the cause of all sensation;
therefore, the mind alone is the self, and never the vital breath.

Based on such experiences as "I am possessed of volition," "I am possessed of thought," and "I am possessed of conceptualization," there exists an inner self, distinct [from the body], which consists of mind (manomaya). ||551||
"Because such scriptural passages exist, the nature of the mind as the Self is logical"—this conviction of his another dull-witted person refutes. (552)
How can the mind be the self when it is an instrument, like the eye and other organs?
An instrument is to be employed by an agent; it does not function by itself. (553)
The agent who employs the instruments is alone worthy of being the self;
the self is an independent person and is never to be employed by another. (554)
Even from the experience "I am the doer," "I am the enjoyer," and "I am happy," the intellect (buddhi) indeed becomes the self (ātman), for the sense of ego (ahaṃkṛti) is a property of the intellect.
The Veda declares that there is another inner self consisting of consciousness (vijñānamaya),
and it describes this self, which consists of consciousness, as having the nature of an agent, distinct even from the mind.

"Consciousness performs the sacrifice and also performs ritual acts"—thus, its agency is directly established by the Śruti. Therefore, the Buddhist concludes that the nature of the self belongs to the intellect (buddhi). //557//
Both the Prābhākara and the Tārkika, out of resentment, refute that determination [of the opponent], asking: "How indeed can cognition be the self? (558)
Because cognition is an effect of ignorance and is perishable, and because all things such as cognition are seen to dissolve into ignorance at every moment. ||559||
From the experience "I am ignorant," which is common even among women and children,
it follows that the self is indeed ignorance itself, and never the intellect.
The Veda also declares that the Self consisting of bliss is distinct from the Self consisting of consciousness, stating: "There is another inner Self, consisting of bliss. (561)
Because it is empty of the conditions for suffering, it is considered to consist of bliss;
in ignorance, as in deep sleep, the intellect and all other faculties dissolve away. (562)
Therefore, even those who are suffering possess a state of being composed of bliss during deep sleep;
furthermore, the experience "I know nothing at all" is observed during sleep. (563)
Since this is so, it is indeed logical that ignorance is certainly the self;
thus, the Bhāṭṭas refute that certainty with their own arguments. (564)
How can ignorance itself be the self, and how is knowledge perceived?
In the absence of knowledge, how could one know the state of ignorance, thinking "I am ignorant"? [One might say:
"I slept very happily; I was not aware of anything therein. (565)
Thus, even ignorance appears as knowledge among the awakened;
for the Śruti also declares: "He is indeed a mass of pure consciousness, consisting of bliss. (566)
That [intellect] itself declares the dual nature of the self;
the self is considered to possess both conscious and insentient forms, like a firefly. (567)
"An insentient entity, like a jar or a wall, is not composed solely of ignorance"—this certainty of theirs is refuted by another insentient entity. (568)
How can the self consist of both knowledge and ignorance?
For these two are mutually contradictory, like light and darkness. (569)

Neither grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), nor conjunction (*saṃyoga*), nor a common substratum (*samāśraya*) is established between knowledge and ignorance, for they are like darkness and light. (570)
Ignorance, as well as discernment or even the intellect, are its qualities;
yet in deep sleep, not even the slightest thing other than these is perceived.
Is it not the case that the characteristics of the mother and so forth are perceived as being merely empty?
For in deep sleep there is nothing else at all, following the realization: "I did not even exist. (572)
When all people have arisen from sleep, they remember only emptiness;
therefore, the self is indeed emptiness, and not characterized by knowledge or ignorance.
Since it is clearly stated even in the Veda that "in the beginning this was indeed non-existent," therefore the nature of emptiness alone is considered the Self. (574)
Only a jar that already exists in a latent state is seen coming into being;
for a pot does not arise from within and emerge toward the outside as something previously non-existent. (575)
Since all this that exists has arisen from that which is non-existent, therefore it is logical that the nature of the void alone constitutes the self of all things. (576)

Thus, by those who consider themselves wise but are mutually contradictory, [the truth is obscured] through their respective limited learning, reasoning, and experiences that conform to their own particular doctrines. (577)
The various systems of tenets have been definitively refuted by the wise;
moreover, they are contradicted for the opponents by both scripture and direct experience. (578)
Therefore, the selflessness of everything from one's son to the ultimate void has been well-established through scripture, reasoning, and direct experience. (579)
For the wise do not accept as corresponding to reality that which is sublated by another means of valid cognition.
Therefore, it is well-established and clear that everything from sons up to the void is of the nature of non-self. (580)

O disciple, at the time of deep sleep, when all [phenomena] have ceased, nothing other than the void (śūnya) is perceived here; that void is you, the Self. Beyond that, no object designated as "Self" is experienced. (581)
If the self exists, why is it not perceived? What is the proof for how it remains during sleep?
What are its characteristics, and how is it that it itself is not sublated while the notions of "I" and so forth are being sublated? (582)
O Guru, out of compassion, sever with the edge of the great sword of reasoning this collection of doubts that has become a knot in my heart. (583)
The venerable Guru said: "This question of yours is considered most subtle and worthy;
for it is only one with a subtle intellect who perceives subtle meanings. (584)
Listen, I shall explain everything that you have now asked—
the supreme, subtle secret that must be known by those seeking liberation.
The entire complex of intellect and the rest, during deep sleep, is dissolved into its own cause;
it remains within the unmanifest, like a banyan tree within its seed, in an unmodified state.
The world does not exist as a void, but rather abides in its own essential nature;
just as a banyan tree exists in some places in the form of a sprout and in others in the form of a seed, so too does that [world] abide in the form of cause and effect. (587)
The Śruti declares that the state of the world is one of an unmanifest nature during deep sleep and other such conditions, as in the passage: "Then, indeed, this was unmanifest. (588)
Without understanding this truth determined through scripture and reasoning, those who do not know it declare that the vision of the world is empty. (589)
The arising of the existent from the non-existent is neither heard in scripture nor observed in experience.
Does anything ever emerge from a human horn, or will anything ever come from a sky-flower? (590)
If a jar does not exist [prior to its production], it cannot arise from clay; rather, let it arise from sand, or from water, or even from nothing at all.
Yet, it never arises from those [latter] in any way whatsoever; therefore, whatever object originates from a particular source, that is its inherent nature (*svabhāva*). (591)
Otherwise, the definition of cause and effect would be reversed;
yet it is fixed in all treatises, in all worlds, and in every respect. (592)
"How can that which is non-existent give rise to the existent? This is refuted by scripture;
therefore, the production of the existent from the non-existent is not possible, and the meaning of the word 'void' (śūnya) is merely false. (593)
While the Prājña state, designated as the unmanifest (avyakta), exists as the true Self and remains awake here, how can emptiness (śūnyatva) be established for that crest-jewel of the deluded? (594)
By which person was it asserted that in deep sleep there is only emptiness?
By what reason was it inferred, and how was it known? Let it be told by you. (595)
Being asked this, what answer will the most foolish person give?
There is no corresponding mark [of inference], nor is there anyone at all to speak it.
For one who is as void as one situated in deep sleep, who else could be the knower of that Self other than himself? (596)
One speaks of that state of emptiness which exists during one's own sleep as something experienced by oneself;
yet therein, the deluded person fails to perceive their own true existence.
He declares that even his own [self] consists of emptiness. ||597||
Not being perceived by himself or by other people, he directly experiences the state of deep sleep;
and he who is the cognizer here of the absence of the intellect and its functions is the witness.
That very self is indeed changeless. ||598||
For that self-luminous one by whose splendor all this shines, what illuminator could there be here—since all things such as intellect are insentient?
Indeed, no illuminator of the sun is seen upon the surface of the earth; and it is exactly the same for the Self.
There is no other illuminator whatsoever, nor any experiencer other than this; there is nothing else beyond this.
By whom is all this experienced in the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep?
Who indeed, and in what manner, can know this knower? (600)
Fire is the burner of everything, and there is no other burner than fire;
just so, for the self which is the knower, no knower whatsoever is perceived. 601.
By whom could this perceiver be perceived?
Since there is no other perception [to perceive it], this self is not perceived. (602)
Due to the dissolution of the objects of cognition such as the intellect and so forth, this one alone does not see, hear, or know anything during deep sleep;
he is himself the witness of the darkness of the state of deep sleep.
Having become thus, he remains here at ease and free from conceptual construction. ||603||
O best of scholars, the supreme authority for the existence of the self during deep sleep is known to be one's own recognition, which is accepted by everyone from children to the elderly. (604)
Because it is recognized [upon waking], the mere mark (liṅga) infers the existence of that which was being remembered; this is the cognition "I slept happily. (605)
"If there were no prior experience, there would be no arising of memory"—such logical reasoning and others constitute the proof for the existence of the self. (606)
That state where there is the cognition of the Self as being free from desire,
and which is independent even of dreams— that is deep sleep;
thus is the existence of the Self proclaimed here.
Therefore, even according to scripture, scripture itself is the authority in this matter.
Since there is no desiring subject in a dream, how can seeing be possible? Therefore, the existence of the self is understood from that [dream]. (608)
By these means of valid cognition, this Self is known by the wise as existing in its capacity as a witness; it is solitary, pure, and characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss. (609)

The truth of the inner self, characterized by existence, consciousness, bliss, and so forth, consists in its being uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time by virtue of its eternal nature. (610)
The state of being pure consciousness is called *cittva* (consciousness-ness) because its nature is knowledge;
it is described as *ānanda* (bliss) because its nature is indivisible happiness. ||611||
||30 ||The Characteristic of the Eternal.
The existence of the self, which is woven through the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, persists as "I am"; therefore, this self is eternal and immutable.
The unbroken cognition "I have always existed" is observed;
because [one never thinks] "I did not exist at any time," the eternity of this self is maintained. (613)

Whether childhood and its various stages have arrived or passed away, and whether all other states of consciousness—whether waking or otherwise—are corrupted or uncorrupted, the singular identity of the Witness, "I am I," remains forever constant; for its essence persists like water within the succession of waves in the Ganges.
The moments beginning with "I" are distinct and subject to change due to their momentary transformation;
however, this Self does not undergo transformation because it is partless, and precisely because it is unchanging, it is eternal.

"I am the very same one who saw the dream and who slept happily; now I am awake"—in this way, the existence of the Self is experienced without interruption; indeed, there is no doubt in this matter. (616)
The sixteen kalās mentioned in the Śruti are the reflection of consciousness (cit) and not of the Self;
because the Self is partless (niṣkala), there is no dissolution of it, and therefore the Self is eternal.
The nature of consciousness.
The sun, which illuminates inert objects, is itself of the nature of light and not inert;
therefore, that which illumines the intellect and other faculties is likewise held to be of the nature of consciousness. 618.

Manifestation from itself is never possible for insentient things such as walls; this is directly perceived everywhere except when there is the light of the sun or other sources. Likewise, even the intellect and its derivatives possess not even an atom of self-luminous manifestation in the absence of the Self.
Thus, this very sun of the one who possesses the Vedic revelation consisting of pure consciousness appears as if it were composed of suffering.

Just as the sun does not desire even the slightest other light for its own manifestation or for the manifestation of other objects, so too this Supreme Self, the element of consciousness, does not require anything else for its own awakening or for the awakening of the "I" and so forth. ||620||

Since this [consciousness] shines by its own nature without depending on any other light, therefore this conscious self is self-luminous; for in the manifestation of its own being, it has no need for the light of another. (621)
That which even the sun does not illuminate, nor the moon, nor lightning, much less this fire of limited luster;
that very Self, which shines while the entire world shines after it, manifests spontaneously in all states.
||32 The Nature of Bliss||
Blissfulness is the specific characteristic of the Self, which is of the nature of happiness;
the Self is of the nature of happiness because it is the object of supreme love. (623)
In all beings, attachment toward the causes of happiness is seen to be limited; however, there is never any limit to living beings' attachment toward their own selves at any time. (624)
For one whose faculties have faded, who is aged, or who has reached the point of departure,
there remains hope only for life, because one's own self is most dear.
Therefore, the self is the object of supreme love for all embodied beings;
it is because of its status as the remainder (the goal) that everything else becomes worthy of being accepted. //626//
This very self is dearer than a son, dearer than wealth, and dearer than everything else; it is the supreme innermost [self]. (627)
That which is regarded as dear is never disliked by men;
for neither in misfortune nor in prosperity is another like oneself. (628)

Indeed, the self is most dear to those who possess life, for the sake of which there exist objects such as wife, children, acquired home, and wealth, as well as various activities such as trade, agriculture, cattle-rearing, royal service, medicine, and so forth. (629)

Whatever activity there is, whether engagement or withdrawal, and whatever movement there may be, it is for the sake of the self alone and not for the sake of anything else; therefore, nothing is dearer than the self.
Therefore, the Self, which is said to be of the nature of absolute bliss and dearer than every other object—
whosoever considers anyone else to be dear [to him], [he does not know].
Therefore, he experiences only sorrow. ||631||
"Another question is posed by me as a disciple; may it be forgiven, O Lord.
The speech of the ignorant leads to transgression, but not that of the great-souled ones. (632)
The self is one thing and happiness another; the self does not have the nature of happiness.
Yet every person strives for the happiness that is desired for the self. (633)
If the self is of the nature of bliss, why then do embodied beings exert effort?
O Lord, may this doubt of mine be dispelled through Your very compassion. (634)
An object that causes suffering is not capable of bestowing happiness.
The venerable Guru says:
An ordinary person, not knowing the Self whose nature is bliss, strives for external pleasure; but no wise man who possesses knowledge does so. (635)
Indeed, it is only because he is unaware of the treasure that the foolish man wanders for alms;
for what wise person, knowing a treasure to be in his own house, would wander for alms? (636)

Having grasped as one's own self the gross and subtle body—which by its very nature consists of suffering—and having forgotten that one's own true nature is happiness, the ignorant person seeks pleasure from those things that bestow only pain. (637)
An object that causes suffering is not capable of bestowing happiness;
does poison grant immortality to a living being who drinks it? (638)
Having determined that the self is one thing and happiness another, the fool strives for external pleasure; this is indeed the truth, there is no doubt. (639)
The bliss that is experienced here by all embodied beings during the enjoyment of desired objects through meditation, vision, and so forth— [640]
That is not a property of the object; therefore, it is perceived only in the mind.
How could there be a perception of a property of the object within the mind? (641)
Elsewhere, however, the perception of other properties is not observed;
therefore, this [absence] is never a property of a real entity, but is rather bliss. (642)
Nor is this phenomenon [of cognition] a property of the mind when the object is non-existent, because it is not observed [to arise then].
One should not think that "the manifested does not arise when the manifestor is absent. (643)
Moreover, even when the object is real, that bliss characterized as previously described does not arise;
for it is not accepted that the manifest can fail to appear even when the manifestor is present. (644)
One should not postulate "bad fortune" (duradṛṣṭa) and the like as an obstacle here; for when a beloved object is obtained, bad fortune does not prevail. (645)
Therefore, mental dharma does not arise from the self because the self is devoid of qualities;
rather, it arises from the proximity of merit and also from an object that has been presided over [by it]. (646)
In this mind, which is dominated by the quality of sattva, the Self itself is reflected, characterized by bliss, like the moon in clear water. (647)
This very manifestation of bliss which is reflected in the mind becomes high or low by itself, according to the excellence or deficiency of one's merit.
That which has been established by the Śruti, beginning with the universal sovereign (sārvabhauma) and ending with Brahmā, is perishable and subject to degrees of excellence;
it undergoes dissolution when its cause is exhausted.
This is the bliss of the sense objects which has merit as its sole means;
those who perform meritorious deeds enjoy this very bliss of the sense objects. (650)
Even at the time of enjoyment, there is suffering, and it becomes even greater at the end; pleasure conjoined with sense objects is like food mixed with poison. (651)
Even at the time of enjoyment, and at the end of enjoyment, it yields nothing but suffering;
for pleasure is subject to fluctuation and is accompanied by the fear of its own perishability.

Just as a gradation is recognized among men who enjoy the fruits of their merit—those who have attained the status of Brahmā and others, and those who have entered royal positions—at the time of their enjoyment [of results], so it is here. (653)
In the same way, even for living beings who attain the status of Brahmā and other such ranks, sensual pleasure is not to be desired by the wise; therefore, indeed, [it is not to be sought]. (654)
That bliss which has become the image, Ānanda, is characterized by the bliss of the Self;
it is eternal, non-dual, full, constant, one, and fearless. ||655||

It is perceived through its reflection, which is like the bliss of an appearance, just as an original object [is known] by its reflection; for the reflection is rooted in the original object and cannot be established without that original object. ||656||
That bliss which is the original object (*bimba*) is perceived through its reflection; it is by means of this very logic that it is understood by wise people, and never otherwise experienced. (657)

The Self, which was previously described as being within the aggregate of the body and organs produced by ignorance, does not exist even in the waking state; it is not an object of perception, just as in a dream. //658//
Even when the gross and subtle body, which is of the nature of suffering,
dissolves in deep sleep, that which is characterized by inward bliss shines forth.
For here there is no object whatsoever, nor anything such as the intellect and so forth;
the Self alone remains, non-dual, consisting of pure bliss. (660)
This [self] is recognized by all people upon waking from sleep as being nothing but bliss; you should not entertain any doubt in this matter. (661)
You too have recognized that the self consists of pure bliss, following upon rising from deep sleep with the recollection, "I slept happily. (662)
As for what was stated by the opponent— that the absence of suffering is happiness—
that is a hollow and false statement from one who has not even smelled the Upaniṣads.
The absence of suffering, however, exists in things such as clods of earth but is not experienced;
whereas even a mere trace of pleasure is indeed directly perceived by everyone. (664)
Introducing this very [Self] as "the Existent," the Śruti declares:
"This is the mass of Existence (saddhana), this is the mass of Consciousness (ciddhana), and this is also the mass of Bliss (ānandaghana). (665)
The nature of this inner self is a mass of bliss;
it is described by blessed, high-souled, steadfast, and most excellent knowers of Brahman. (666)
In meditative absorption, the Self is experienced through direct perception alone; thus, it is as nothing but pure bliss—of this there is no doubt. (667)
Brahmā and all other living beings subsist upon a mere fraction of this very [bliss], characterized as bliss, in accordance with their respective limiting adjuncts (upādhi). (668)
That sweet taste which produces pleasure when tasted among foods belongs to the molasses alone; those [other substances] possess sweetness nowhere at all. (669)

In the same way, the bliss that is perceived due to the proximity of an object is merely a flash of a portion of the bliss of the original image (bimba); it does not belong to those whose nature is insentient.
Whichever bliss is perceived through whatever means, wherever it may be, that is indeed the manifestation of the supreme Brahman. 671.
Just as the blossoming of the night-lotus is solely due to the grace of the moon,
so too the arising of bliss for these [beings] occurs only through the manifestation of the ultimate reality.
||34 ||The state of being without a second.

The *sattva* of the mind is likewise the very nature of bliss belonging to the Supreme Self; yet, because the attributeless [Self] is not joined with qualities (*guṇa*), those qualities do not exist for it. (673)
A qualification serves for the purpose of exclusion only when there exists another substance;
however, this Supreme Self is non-dual because the phenomenal world is illusory. (674)
Because there is no other entity [to serve as its counter-correlate], it is never excluded; thus, being "alone" and "without qualities" is defined as its qualitylessness. (675)
Even upon being heard, their status as qualities is not established for [the self],
just as heat and light belong to fire, so it is with the self.
It is certain that the essential nature consists of existence, consciousness, bliss, and so forth;
for this very reason, it is characterized by being both similar and dissimilar [to other things]. (677)
No distinction exists in the non-dual supreme Self, which is the reality;
any division produced by a different nature arises only through the negation of phenomenal proliferation (prapañca). //678//
That mode is not accepted; I shall explain it to you, so listen with respect.
[It is] that which, in reality, consists merely of the qualities (guṇa) as a transformation of the qualities. (679)
Those who perceive non-dual Brahman declare that the vision of this world of manifestation as being nothing but pure Being is "negation" (apavāda). 680.
This should be understood by those of subtle intellect through the reversal of that [order of arising];
that this perceived world is pure existence (*sanmātra*) is established by sound reasonings. (681)

One should perceive this entire, most gross cosmic egg as consisting merely of the fivefold-compounded elements (pañcīkṛtabhūta): the fourfold collection of gross bodies, their food such as grain, and their substrata. 682.

Whatever is perceived in the form of an effect, when investigated here, is found to be nothing but that [cause] itself; for example, a jar or other such things produced from clay, when properly investigated, do not differ from the clay. (683)
Both inside and out, only clay is perceived; nothing such as a jar exists apart from clay.
That which possesses a neck and so forth is the jar, and it is thus [identical to its material].
Nor should it be said that this is merely earth and nothing else.
In its true nature, it is merely clay that is designated by ignorant people with names such as "water-pot" and so forth;
for while there is a difference in name, there is no difference in the actual substance.
It is clearly perceived when that is being investigated. ||685||
Therefore, indeed, an effect is never different from its own cause; for this reason,
my dear, all that is composed of the elements is likewise so.
That is merely that [state], and not distinct from it either. ||686||

Moreover, all this— the collection of quintuplicated elements together with their respective qualities such as sound, as well as the subtle bodies— becomes nothing but the non-quintuplicated elements alone.
That collection of unevolved elements,
together with the qualities of rajas, tamas, and sattva,
becomes by its very nature mere unmanifest (avyakta).
And this unmanifest [nature] itself possesses appearance. ||688||
That too, along with the collection of unevolved elements and the qualities of rajas, tamas, and sattva,
is that which is undivided and primordial, serving as the substratum.
The supreme Brahman is pure and eternally of one form; it exists as pure being alone, and there is no conceptualization beyond that which is real—it is the one all-encompassing reality. (689)

Just as the single moon appears to have a second due solely to a defect in a person's vision, so too does Brahman appear manifold through the defect of the intellect; when that defect is destroyed, the reality shines as one alone. (690)

Just as the cognition of a snake, once the true nature of the rope has been apprehended, dissolves into that very rope, so too the perception of the world, through the realization of Brahman, dissolves into that very [Brahman] along with the delusion. (691)
Through the complete pacification of the mind that perceives duality arising from error, there exists only that which is eternally one and eternally non-dual;
therefore, no distinction created by a different nature exists here within the non-conceptual Brahman. 692.
When there is an adjunct (*upādhi*), the Self, being non-different from it, then appears as if it were of the same class (*sajātīya*).

Since its nature is false due to its being like the objects of a dream, when that [adjunct] is no longer perceived, this very Self attains oneness with Brahman; it does not appear as separate. Therefore, there is no distinction created by anything of the same class. ||693||
Just as the space within a jar becomes the great space when the jar is absent, so too,
in the absence of limiting adjuncts, this Self is itself nothing but absolute Brahman.
Space is always full, whether the jar exists or does not exist;
by what means can the fragmentation of the eternally full sky be established? (695)
To the ignorant, the uninterrupted [space] appears as if cut by objects such as jars, just as the earth appears divided by boundaries such as villages and fields. (696)
In the very same way, the supreme Brahman, the greatest among the great, appears as if limited due to delusion and the objects imagined by it. (697)
Therefore, the difference between Brahman and the Self is imagined, not real;
for this very reason, the Śruti repeatedly establishes their identity. (698)

For the sake of establishing the non-duality of Brahman and the Self through the formula "That thou art," the identity of the literal meanings (vācya) of the terms *tat* and *tvam* is not applicable due to contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge; rather,
the unity of the referents (lakṣya) of those two terms alone is established.
O Master, how many kinds of meanings are considered for the two words *tat* and *tvam*?
What indeed is the denoted meaning (*vācyārtha*) of each word, and what is the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*) of both together? (700)
If one intends to express the oneness of the expressed meanings, what contradiction is perceived? And if the indicated meanings are non-different, how can that contradiction be removed? (701)
What figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) has been accepted here in speaking of oneness? Please explain all of this correctly out of compassion. (702)
The meaning of the two words "That" (tat) and "Thou" (tvam).
Listen attentively, O learned one; today your ascetic penance has borne fruit.
By merely hearing these words, perfect knowledge shall arise.
As long as the meaning of the two words "That" and "Thou" is not properly investigated, for that long alone does bondage—characterized by death and worldly existence—persist for human beings. (704)
The state [of liberation] consists of the single, indivisible essence of being, consciousness, and bliss;
for the virtuous, liberation is attained through the immediate, direct realization of the meaning of the Great Saying. 705.
The meaning of the sentence alone must be understood by one seeking liberation for the sake of release from worldly existence.
Therefore, becoming attentive, listen; I shall speak it in brief. (706)

The meanings of sentences have been declared by the most excellent of scholars to be manifold, distinguished as the expressed (vācya), the indicated (lakṣya), and so forth; listen now to that which is relevant to the present context.
In the sentence "That thou art," there are three words;
among them, that which exists at the beginning—the word *tat*—is now being explained. (708)
The correct meaning of that term is as follows.
Those skilled in the meaning of the treatises state that the meaning is twofold: the expressed (*vācya*) and the indicated (*lakṣya*).
I shall explain to you the expressed meaning as it has been articulated by the learned. (709)
Ignorance in its collective form (sāmāsa), augmented by the quality of sattva,
is accompanied by its own effects, beginning with the ether and ending with Virāṭ.
Consciousness, when delimited by that [power], is characterized by truth, knowledge, and so forth, and is endowed with qualities such as omniscience, lordship, and being the inner controller. ||711||
That which possesses the attributes of being the creator, protector, and destroyer of the world, which manifests as the self of all, and which is immeasurable even by its own qualities; //712//
The unmanifest, supreme Brahman is said to be the expressed meaning (vācyārtha), just as there is a syntactic connection of the sentence-meaning in the expression "a blue lotus. (713)

Likewise, in the case of "That thou art," there is no logical consistency in the meaning of the sentence; for a blue object, when qualified by the word "lotus," is distinguished from other blue things such as cloth. (714)
The blue lotus is distinguished from whiteness by its blueness;
thus, through their mutual exclusion, they function as the differentiators of one another. (715)
Whether the sentence-meaning consists of the qualifier-qualified relation or some other type of relation,
there is no contradiction with other means of valid cognition.
Therefore, the meaning of the sentence is properly established as being free from contradiction;
however, in this way, the meaning of the sentence "That thou art" (tattvamasi) is not consistent.
Of that [first] object, which is consciousness qualified by mediacy and so forth; and of the "thou" (tvam) object, which is consciousness qualified by immediacy and so forth. ||718||
In the same way, because they mutually differentiate one another, there is either a qualifier-qualified relationship, a relation of conjunction, or some other [relation] between those two. (719)

If it were the meaning of a sentence, there would be contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge; therefore, the meaning of the sentence is not tenable. I shall explain that contradiction to you. (720)
By virtue of qualities such as being the Lord of all, absolute independence, and omniscience,
the Lord is the supreme of all, whose desires are true and whose volitions are true.

The referent of "That" (tatpadārtha) is the Self, while the referent of "Thou" (tvamartha) is this transmigrating individual soul (jīva), who possesses limited knowledge, leads a life of suffering, follows the course of that [world], and is characterized by material nature (prākṛta). ||722||
How can oneness be possible for these two opposites?
This contradiction between both is perceived through direct perception.

Because they are pervaded by contradictory attributes, the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa) are mutually distinct, like fire and snow, both in terms of their verbal expression and their referents.

If their identity were abandoned on the grounds that it would contradict perception and other means of valid cognition, there would arise a great contradiction with the words of the Śruti and a contradiction with the words of the Smṛti. ||725||
The dependence of these two upon the Śruti is stated as its primary purport;
therefore, the word of the Śruti, "That thou art," must be accepted repeatedly. (726)
Furthermore, whether the sentence-meaning consists of a qualified entity or a relation,
because it would be non-conformable with reality, this [sentence-meaning] is not accepted as the meaning of the Veda.
The meaning of the sentence, as accepted by the Śruti, is its indivisible single flavor;
moreover, the gross and subtle phenomenal world is repeatedly declared to be pure Being alone. (728)
Having demonstrated that the self is non-different from Brahman during deep sleep, and having established this, [the author] desires to demonstrate the eternal oneness [of all things]. //729//
Having already stated that "all this has that as its self," the Śruti declares the identity of Being (sat) and the Self (ātman) for the sake of establishing the non-duality of Brahman.
As long as there is conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) or a living soul (*jīva*), how can there be non-duality (*advaitatva*) for Brahman?
Therefore, their indivisibility and oneness are what is sanctioned by the Śruti. (731)
By abandoning the contradictory portions, perception and the other means of knowledge do not sublate [the scripture];
by grasping the non-contradictory portions, it is not contradicted even by the Śruti.
The inapplicability of the literal meaning.
Indication (lakṣaṇā) must be accepted for the sake of establishing the meaning of the sentence;
indication is indeed resorted to precisely because the literal meaning is untenable. (733)
The wise have declared that *lakṣaṇā* (indication) occurs when the primary connection [of the literal meaning] is untenable;
this is considered the *jahallakṣaṇā* (exclusive indication) found in expressions such as "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā. (734)
This [notion of] the relationship between locus and located, characterized as that of the Ganges and the hamlet on its bank, does not apply here in the sentence "That thou art. (735)
Therefore, because every contradictory meaning of the sentence is [subsequently] contradicted by perception,
figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) operates there, just as it does regarding the bank's connection with the Gaṅgā.
Likewise, when the intended meaning of the sentence "That thou art" (tattvamasi) is the unity of consciousness, [the nature of that] is characterized by immediacy and so forth. ||737||
Only the literal meaning (bhāgyamātra) is contradicted, but not everything;
therefore, the application of exclusive indication (jahallakṣaṇā) is not appropriate here. ||738||
If the entire literal meaning were abandoned, no fruit would be seen for human beings, just as one might perceive nothing but hardness in a coconut fruit. (739)
Just as the word "Ganges" abandons its own primary meaning and indicates the riverbank,
so too do the words "That" (tat-pada) or "Thou" (tvam-pada) abandon their entire respective primary meanings.
If it itself indicates either the meaning of "that" (tad) or the meaning of "thou" (tvam), then the operation of jahallakṣaṇā is logically established. ||741||

It should not be suspected that there is no figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) when the meaning is known by the noble ones; for either the word "that" (tat-pada) or the word "thou" (tvam-pada) is both heard and understood [in such contexts]. (742)
And for that purpose, how could figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) operate there?
In this case, it does not operate, just as in the sentence "The red [horse] runs. //743//
Or it may be a non-exclusive indication (*ajahallakṣaṇā*), just as it is an exclusive indication (*jahallakṣaṇā*);
for in the world, the movement of a quality is impossible without a substance. (744)

Therefore, without abandoning that [primary meaning], the "indicated" (lakṣya) and so forth—characterized by being the locus of its qualities—is indicated; thus, this secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) operates therein.
In the sentence "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), which conveys the unity of Brahman and the self, there are two aspects of consciousness characterized by mediacy and immediacy, respectively. (746)
Since the sentence-meaning consisting of oneness cannot be established because of the exclusion of contradictory parts, therefore the non-abandoning indication (ajahallakṣaṇā) is not accepted.

Having completely abandoned those parts of the "That-word" (tat-pada) and the "Thou-word" (tvam-pada) that are contradictory to their own respective meanings, [they remain] joined with those parts that are not so contradictory. ||748||

For one who correctly perceives either the meaning of "that" (tad) or the meaning of "thou" (tvam) by themselves through partial indication (bhāgalakṣaṇā), let there be no doubt as to whether there is anything further to be accomplished. //749//
How can a single word, through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), be capable of indicating both a portion that is another entity—which is non-contradictory—and its own portion? [750]
When the cognition of the word-meaning has been established by itself through another word, why would there be a further dependence on that meaning for a figurative indication (lakṣaṇā)? [751]
Therefore, in the statement "That thou art," it is held that there is a secondary figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) of the type known as "indication by parts" (bhāgalakṣaṇā),
for the purpose of establishing the reality of the sentence-meaning as an indivisible, single essence.
When a contradictory part is abandoned and non-contradiction is indicated, those who are experts in the science of indication call that "indication by parts" (bhāgalakṣaṇā). ||753||
The sentence "This is Devadatta," or even its meaning,
does not convey its own sentential object, which is the single form of Devadatta.

Having set aside the contradictory factor—the specific distinctions of place, time, and so forth—the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) is simply the body of Devadatta, which is non-contradictory. [755]

Just as one correctly characterizes [an object] by means of this [sentence] through part-characterization (*bhāgalakṣaṇā*), so too in the case of the sentence "That thou art," either the sentence itself or the meaning of the sentence [functions in this way]. (756)

In the case of two cognitions characterized by such qualities as being indirect or direct, that aspect which is presented as contradictory to the meaning of the sentence—namely, their identity—is [to be negated]. (757)
Characterized by being beyond perception, not beyond perception, omniscience, and so forth,
everything from the intellect (*buddhi*) down to the gross body is rooted in ignorance (*avidyā*) and is non-self (*anātman*).
Having abandoned the contradictory portions, the reality characterized by pure consciousness is solely existence itself—free from conceptual construction and untainted. (759)
38. The Concordance of Meanings.
Therefore, by means of this correct characteristic of fortune,
one perceives that which is free from all limiting adjuncts— the non-dual reality of Being, Consciousness, and Bliss.

Without distinction, without appearance, unlike anything seen, unlike anything else, indefinable, without beginning or end, infinite, peaceful, and immutable— Brahman, which is beyond reasoning and unknowable, devoid of qualities, remains as the residue.

The contradiction between Brahman and the self is produced by the distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); through the realization of their oneness, once the distinction of limiting adjuncts is cast aside, there is no contradiction whatsoever between these two. (762)

Their limiting adjuncts, their qualified state, their participation in those attributes, and their distinctness—all this is produced by delusion and is utterly false, like the objects of a dream; it is not real even in the waking state. (763)

Neither the manifold expansion of sleep, the body, its attributes, pleasure, pain, and so forth, nor even the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa), can ever be established as real; such is the delusion regarding space, time, the world, the Lord, and so on, which is merely imagined through māyā.
What difference is there between these two? Which one would be the truth as opposed to the other? ||764||

No distinction whatsoever is observed between the states of dreaming and waking by means of conceptual constructions born of delusion; for this very reason, they are false, consisting as they do of the perception of what has already been seen.
Indeed, waking is exactly like a dream. //765//
Both dream and waking are equal insofar as they are effects of ignorance;
in both cases, the conceptualization of the seer, the seeing, and the seen is the same. (766)

The absence of both [dream and waking] is experienced by everyone during deep sleep; there is no difference whatsoever between these two, and therefore, the dream state deserves to be considered false.
O wise one, this distinction within Brahman characterized by similarity and so forth is merely due to delusion; in reality, not even the slightest distinction exists across the three periods of time.
The scriptural passage, "where one sees nothing else," negates duality;
it does so in order to bring about the realization of the falsity of that which is imagined through delusion within the plenum (bhūman).

Therefore, Brahman is eternally non-dual, devoid of conceptual construction, free from limiting adjuncts, stainless, a solid mass of uninterrupted bliss, effortless, supportless, and solely one without a second. //770//
There is no distinction whatsoever, no perception of qualities, nor even the activity of speech or the activity of the mind;
for there shines forth only that which is absolute, supremely peaceful, infinite, primordial, pure bliss, and non-dual reality. //771//
This is the supreme truth, the reality whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss; it is ageless, immortal, and eternal—this is my true word. (772)
For you are not the body, nor the vital breaths, nor even the collection of senses, nor the mind, nor the intellect, nor anywhere the ego-sense;
nor are you a mere aggregate of these. Listen further, O wise one.
That which is their stainless radiance as witness is indeed your true self. ||773||
Whatever entity is born, that very thing grows and that same thing meets its death in due time;
yet for that which is eternal, all-pervading, and unborn, there is neither birth nor indeed death.
This very outpouring that has been produced thrives and perishes through the application of karma;
you, however, remaining as pure consciousness alone, shall witness it throughout all its various states. (775)

That which is self-luminous, whose nature is the entirety [of existence], which shines eternally as "I, I" through a single essence from deep sleep onwards, which is the unchanging witness of the intellect and all its modifications—that Brahman, the reality, you are; you are pure consciousness alone. (776)
It bestows existence upon the entire universe, beginning with space, which is imagined within its own consciousness that never sets;
it directly extends manifestation through its own splendor.
That which is Brahman is "Thou art That," consisting solely of pure consciousness.

Those belonging to the lineage of the supreme *paramahaṃsas*, whose inner selves are stainless and who delight in right concentration, behold their own reality— boundless bliss— directly and are perpetually satisfied.
That which is Brahman, "Thou art That," is pure consciousness alone.

That Brahman which is within and without, itself undivided and of a single form, rises up before the deluded intellect as if it were an object superimposed—like clay and other such things—yet remains devoid of modification and is to be known by the Self; that Brahman, which is pure consciousness alone, you are. (779)
