That Brahman which is declared by the Vedas—immutable, infinite, without beginning, middle, or end, unmanifest, imperishable, without support, immeasurable, consisting of the wealth of bliss, free from disease, and non-dual—that reality you are, which is pure consciousness alone. (780)
This superimposition of a body, its connection [to it], and its attributes upon you occurs through the power of delusion;
in reality, none of this exists. Therefore, you are unborn, what fear of death can there be for you, and you are the Absolute Fullness.
Whatever is seen by your own deluded vision, that very thing is You alone when seen through the vision of reality as it truly is.
Since there is no object whatsoever in the world other than You, how could fear arise for You, who are non-dual? (782)
For the wise person who perceives "I am indeed all this" through the Self, from what could fear arise? Why is it not accepted that there is no fear of oneself? (783)
Therefore, you are eternally fearless, characterized by absolute bliss, partless, actionless, peaceful, and indeed Brahman itself, forever non-dual. (784)

Knowledge that is devoid of knower, means of knowing, and object to be known; knowledge that is non-different from the knower and undivided; pure and awakened reality, free from such notions as "knowable" and "unknowable"—that you are. 785.

That which is untouched by conceptual constructions such as "inner consciousness" and so forth, which is pure seeing alone, mere existence, the single flavor, the one, the pure and awakened—That Reality you are. //786//

That which is of every form, all, yet not-all, which serves as the ultimate limit for the negation of everything—that reality which is true, eternal, one, infinite, pure, and awakened—thou art that. //787//
You are that Reality—eternal bliss, the undivided single essence, partless, actionless, devoid of modification, non-different from the inner self, the supreme unmanifest, pure, and awakened. (788)
You are that reality which has cast off all distinctions, like the sky, full both within and without—the supreme non-duality, pure bliss of Brahman, pure and awakened; you are That. (789)
"I am indeed Brahman; I am Brahman, devoid of qualities and free from conceptual construction.
Abide thus in the actionless Brahman with an uninterrupted state of awareness. (790)
Never ceasing from this very unbroken state— a wave of realized supreme bliss, pure and having utterly destroyed the cognition of duality—
one should remain incessantly within one's own self, the Supreme Brahman, which is incomparable happiness.
Enjoy yourself; exhaust your *prārabdha* karma through this pleasant way of life.
O wise sage, remaining steadfast in meditative absorption with a mind solely intent on savoring the essence of the bliss of Brahman, abide forever. (792)
O disciple,
does this mental state called "indivisible" arise in the listener merely from hearing the meaning of the sentence, or does it require some other action? ||793||
What is meditative absorption (samādhi)? How many kinds are there? What is the means for its accomplishment?
What are the obstacles to meditative absorption? Let all of this be examined. (794)
||39 ||Section||
The illustrious Guru [states]:
"In this matter, there exist qualified aspirants distinguished as primary, secondary, and so forth;
according to their respective levels of wisdom, the undivided state of consciousness shall arise. (795)
That twice-born one who, having propitiated the Lord through ritual action performed with faith and devotion, has acquired the majesty of His grace even in other births,

and is endowed with the means such as discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal, intense dispassion, and renunciation— he is the preeminent qualified seeker esteemed by the wise for the practice of *śravaṇa*.
When the teacher, following the sequence of superimposition and negation, has here caused the meaning of the sentence to be understood by this person of pure intellect,
who is already existent, that supreme, singular reality— which is eternal bliss, non-dual, incomparable, and stainless— [is realized].
Then there arises the mental modification in the form of supreme non-duality: "I am indeed that Brahman. ||797||

That mental modification (vṛtti), which is of an undivided form and endowed with the reflection of consciousness, takes as its object solely the Supreme Brahman, which is non-different from the Self. ||798||

When ignorance residing therein—which is characterized as an obscuration—is sublated by a cognitive state (*vṛtti*) of undivided form, that ignorance being thus sublated, [the self-luminous nature manifests]. ||799||
Therefore, that entire effect is simultaneously sublated by it, just as when the threads are burned, the cloth which is their effect is likewise burned. (800)
Because it is an effect, its occurrence as the individual soul (jīva) is sublated, just as a mere reflection is incapable of illuminating the sun. ||801||
In the very same way, the consciousness consisting of the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa-caitanya), though residing within a mental modification (vṛtti),
is unable to illuminate the supreme Brahman, which is self-luminous.
Like a lamp placed in the midst of a fierce glare, its rays are extinguished;
being overwhelmed by that splendor, it then becomes withdrawn due to the disappearance of its limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
It becomes solely the mere Supreme Brahman, which is the original object;
just as when a mirror has been removed, the reflected face vanishes of its own accord. ||804||

Just as that [space] would become mere mouth-space, so too does this [consciousness] occur through the destruction of its limiting adjuncts (upādhi), once ignorance regarding the jar has been sublated by the pervasive mental modification (vṛtti). ||805||
This reflection of consciousness causes the jar to shine by its own radiance;
however, such a reflection is not required in Brahman, which is self-luminous.
Therefore, it is held that for real entities, there is pervasion by the mental mode (*vṛtti*), but not pervasion by the fruit (*phala*); thus, there is no mutual contradiction between the two. (807)
Therefore, Brahman, as declared by the Śruti, is to be known through subtle intellect alone;
for those whose wisdom is dull, it does not come about through the mere hearing of the scriptures.

But there may be an undivided mental state (*akhaṇḍākāravṛtti*) even without reflection (*manana*) and so forth, provided there is uninterrupted and devoted hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditation (*dhyāna*). (809)
The intellect attains subtlety, and from that, the object is perceived;
therefore, those of dull intelligence must practice again and again. (810)
Hearing, reflection, and meditation are for the sake of correctly perceiving the reality of the non-dual Existent, by means of the six marks of all Vedānta statements. (811)
They know *śravaṇa* to be the ascertainment of the intended meaning regarding the Supreme Brahman—the very non-dual reality that has been heard, which is the inner self (*pratyagātman*). (812)

Reflective contemplation (*manana*) consists of reflecting upon the meaning of what has been heard by means of reasonings consistent with the statements of Vedānta; it is the cause for the direct realization [of that truth]. (813)
Just as one first abandons conditions such as a body of a different class and then establishes a continuous flow of mental states belonging to the same class. ||814||
That meditation is intended to proceed in an uninterrupted flow like a stream of oil;
for that duration, one should always practice listening with diligent effort. (815)

As long as doubt regarding the means of valid cognition does not cease within one's own mind, so too should doubt regarding the objects of cognition be dispelled through scripture and reasoning. (816)

One must repeatedly engage in reflection for the sake of ascertaining the true nature of the Self; until the contrary notion of the Self is destroyed within the mind, one who desires liberation must practice uninterrupted meditation. (817)

As long as the phenomenal world of the visible has not dissolved through direct realization—even though it has already been refuted by reasoning—so long must this mendicant properly perform meditation and the other [spiritual disciplines]. (818)
Samādhi is both with conceptualization and without conceptualization.

Samādhi is said to be of two kinds: with conceptualization (savikalpa) and without conceptualization (nirvikalpa). I shall state the definition of that which is with conceptualization; listen to it. ||819||
Without the dissolution of the knower and so forth, the mental state remains fixed upon the absolute Brahman, the object of knowledge, by taking on its very form. (820)
That very samādhi with conceptualization (savikalpaka) is to be understood by the wise as being like the appearance of an elephant made of clay, even though only the clay itself is manifest. ||821||
Even when only the reality of pure Being (sanmātra) appears, the threefold division (tripuṭī) shines as consisting of that Being;
for this very reason, this [state] is designated as "savikalpa-samādhi" (concentrated awareness with mental constructs). ||822||

Having abandoned the state of being a knower and so forth, when there is a firm abiding in the object of knowledge alone, the mind becomes free from conceptual construction; this is samādhi, known as yoga. (823)
Salt cast into water remains as nothing but water;
it does not appear separately, but rather only the single water itself is perceived. ||824||
In that very same way, that state of existence remains as nothing but Brahman;
it does not appear as something separate, but rather Brahman alone shines forth as non-dual. //825//
Because it is devoid of conceptual constructions such as "knower" and so forth, this [cognition] is considered non-conceptual;
the distinction between the two is maintained through the presence of the mental mode (vṛtti) and its absence. ||826||
||41 ||The Characteristics of Samādhi||
Among the states of meditative absorption and sleep, it is absorption that is intended here, not sleep;
these two types of absorption—conceptual and non-conceptual—reside in the heart. (827)
For one desiring liberation, these two must be practiced with effort for the sake of turning away from the opposite;
when this is accomplished, there occurs the cessation of contrary mental cultivation. (828)
The unimpeded nature of knowledge and its perpetual bliss are established;
it is considered to be of two kinds: permeated by the visible and permeated by the word. (829)
Listen as I describe the characteristic of those two which involves conceptualization:
it is that wherein association with visible objects of cognition, such as desire and the like, is observed. (830)
This very samādhi, permeated by the object of perception, is *savikalpaka* (conceptual);
it consists of mental fluctuations such as "I," "mine," "this," and so forth, as well as desire, anger, and the like. (831)
By which [the seer] they are seen, by that very [seer] the objects of sight, such as the "I" and so forth, would be perceived;
[he is] the changeless witness of all mental states, beginning with desire. (832)
One should know oneself as the witness who, being inactive, observes those [states];
I am the witness of desire and the rest, for they are seen by me. (833)
Thus, knowing the Self as the witness within oneself, one should dissolve the entire range of objects of perception, such as desire and the like, into one's very own Self. (834)
I am not the body, nor the vital breath, nor the group of senses; I am not the ego, nor the mind, nor even the intellect—
nor am I within those modifications of theirs.
I am the eternal witness, the very inner self. ||835||

He is the witness of speech and the witness of the activity of the vital breath; He is the witness of the intellect and the witness of the activity of the intellect; and He is the witness of the senses, such as the eyes and ears.
I am the eternal witness, indeed the inner self. ||836||
I am neither gross nor subtle; I am neither long, nor am I a child, nor a youth, nor an old man.
I am neither one-eyed, nor mute, nor impotent.
I am the eternal witness, the very inner self. ||837||
I am neither a comer nor a goer, neither a slayer nor an agent, neither an instigator nor a speaker;
I am neither an enjoyer, nor happy, nor indeed miserable.
I am the eternal witness, the very inner self. ||838||
I am neither a yogi nor one separated from yoga; I am neither passionate, nor angry, nor desirous, nor greedy;
I am neither bound, nor joined, nor liberated.
I am the eternal witness, indeed the innermost self. ||839||
He is neither one whose wisdom is within, nor one whose wisdom is without;
he is neither wise nor even unwise.
I am neither a hearer, nor a thinker, nor an awakener.
I am the eternal witness, indeed the innermost self. ||840||
I have no connection with body, senses, or intellect;
I possess not even a trace of merit nor a trace of sin;
I am far removed from the six waves of hunger, thirst, and the rest.
I am eternally liberated, being solely pure consciousness. ||841||
I am without hands or feet, without speech, eyes, or breath; indeed, I am without mind and without intellect.
Like the sky, I am full; I am utterly pure.
I am always of one form, pure consciousness alone. ||842||
Thus, constantly observing his own self and dissolving whatever is perceived as an object of sight,
the wise man abandons all contrary states of being.
That which is perceived as intrinsic nature is [in fact] perceived through the power of delusion. ||843||
The manifestation of the self as something contrary [to its true nature] is itself said to be liberation;
this is accomplished only by one who is always in a state of meditative absorption, and not otherwise. (844)
Liberation is certainly not attained through dress or speech; it is the state of abiding solely as the indivisible conscious self.
To achieve that, one who is always established in one's own self should abandon the sense of "I" and the sense of "mine" regarding limiting adjuncts.
Having firmly grasped the reality of one's own self, one should effect the destruction of primordial nature (prakṛti);
by that alone one becomes liberated, and not otherwise, even by millions of karmas.
"Upon knowing the God, there is the casting off of all bonds;
with the afflictions exhausted, there is the abandonment of birth and death"—
thus indeed does this Vedic speech declare.
Through the destruction of the afflictions, there is the abandonment of birth and death. ||847||
Liberation is the non-occurrence of further birth and so forth;
it shines forth when afflictions are destroyed, as the absence of birth and so forth.
The cause for the destruction of afflictions is one-pointed abidance in the Self.
Therefore, one who desires liberation must indeed establish themselves in the Self. ||848||

The afflictions (kleśas) are merely latent impressions (vāsanās) that serve as the cause for a living being's birth and so forth; when these are consumed by the fire of the perfection of knowledge, they no longer possess the quality of being a cause for rebirth. (849)
Just as seeds scorched by fire do not sprout again, so too the self is not produced again once the afflictions have been consumed by knowledge. 850.

Therefore, one who desires liberation must strive diligently to establish oneself in knowledge, for the sake of completely destroying all latent impressions and for the cessation of contrary tendencies. (851)
For one who is intent upon steadfastness in knowledge, action is of no use;
there can be no coexistence of action and steadfastness in knowledge. (852)
Because they are mutually contradictory and possess distinct natures, action preceded by the cultivation of agency is of a different character from knowledge. (853)
Knowledge is for the purpose of severing the notion of the body as the self, while action serves to increase it;
action is rooted in ignorance, whereas knowledge is the destroyer of fear.
How can the union of action with knowledge be accomplished when they are enemies?
Their coexistence is not possible, just as that of darkness and light. (855)

Just as there is no looking toward the east for those who behold the Inner Self even during the closing and opening of their eyes, so too, for those who perceive the Inner Self, how can there be any perception of the external?
For one whose mind is inclined inward, how can there be any fitness for ritual action? (856)
For the monk who is devoted solely to the state of gnosis, there is indeed no room for the system of ritual action;
for him, that very [gnosis] is the ritual action, that is the twilight rite (sandhyā), and that is everything—there is nothing other than that. //857//
The bathing of the self is the washing away of the impurity imagined by the intellect;
by that alone is its purification, not by clay nor by water. (858)
The establishment of the mind in its own true nature is held to be the spiritual practice;
that which is accomplished by the three instruments is false, because it is unreal. (859)

That state which remains in its own essential nature after having negated the entire visible world is the twilight (sandhyā); its performance is that [state], its giving is that, and indeed its eating is that. (860)
For those holy ones who have realized the ultimate truth, whose nature is that of pure beings, what other practice could there be for ascetics besides their own inner contemplation? (861)
Therefore, having abandoned other activities, the ascetic intent on the perfection of knowledge should remain forever established in the Self, motionless and solely devoted to that. 862.
One who desires to ascend the yoga must perform the action appropriate to oneself;
however, for one who is merely engaged in the act of ascending, that action is not considered true ascent.
For that seeker of liberation who ascends to yoga, even the slightest other action is not appropriate;
one whose mind is attached to another action falls.
It is certain, like one who climbs a palmyra tree. ||864||

For the wise one who has ascended to yoga, who has attained perfection and fulfilled his purpose, there is indeed no outward vision; what then can be said of ritual actions? Samādhi permeated by the visible is called "with conceptual construction" (savikalpaka). ||865||
The truth is to be understood through the Vedas.
I am pure, I am awakened; by my essential nature, I am eternally perfected.
I am peace, I am infinite; I am indeed an ocean of perpetual supreme bliss. (866)

I am the beginning, yet I am without beginning; I am the sole reality to be attained by speech and mind; I am to be known through the words of the Vedas; I am the form of faultless, indivisible consciousness. (867)
I am other than the known and the unknown; I am devoid of even a trace of Māyā and its effects;
I consist solely of pure vision; I am pure consciousness, eternally manifest. (868)
I am without another, I am without what is not another; I am full both within and without.
I am undecaying, I am imperishable, I am eternal bliss, I am without a second. (869)
I am indeed Brahman, the supreme light—the inner, indivisible, pure reality characterized by truth, knowledge, and so forth, which is to be realized through the Vedas and is the ultimate truth. 870.
Thus, with a mental modification (vṛtti) that grasps pure existence, the steadfast ascetic should contemplate the reality presented by words that grasp only that [existence]. (871)
This state belongs to one who is established in the visible world itself, preceded by the dissolution of the visible objects such as desire, and mixed with verbal expressions such as "I am pure."
Meditative concentration is said to be permeated by words. ||872||

Because it is the witness even of that which is visible, and because there is a complete delineation within itself, the state of the mind that brings about cessation is called "non-conceptual" (nirvikalpa). //873//
He who practices conceptual meditative absorption (savikalpa-samādhi) for a long time, continuously, and preceded by mental cultivation, achieves non-conceptual [absorption] (nirvikalpa). ||874||
For one who abides in the perfection of non-conceptual samādhi, permanence certainly arises;
there is the removal of birth and so forth, which is unimpeded.
Possessing eternal, immovable, constant bliss. ||875||
Free from any perception of "I" or "this," whether external or internal, a certain unique being remains silent, immersed in the ocean of the nectar of his own bliss. (876)

Those who are firmly established in that very Supreme Brahman, which is free from conceptual construction— they alone are blessed and liberated, even while living, as compared to those who perceive only the external.
Just as the triad of meditative absorptions is practiced with effort within the heart,
so too should it be performed in the external sphere for the sake of the cessation of duality.
I shall explain that method in brief; listen.
The supreme Brahman, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss, is the substratum. (879)
Therein, this world, consisting of name and form, appears as superimposed;
it is that triad of Brahman which consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss. (880)
The form of the superimposed world is this duality of name and form; these are the five: being, consciousness, bliss, name, and form. (881)
Out of delusion, fools speak of this as "the universe" by treating it as a single entity, just as they name [water] "coldness," "white," "taste," "that which flows," and "wave. (882)
Just as this [wave] is designated by combining [its parts] as "this is a wave," so too, when name and form are superimposed upon the existent Brahman, they are disregarded. (883)
The first external samādhi is the grasping of the mere essential nature;
it is the withdrawal [of the mind] from Brahman, whose nature is existence-consciousness-bliss. (884)

Having separated name and form and dissolving them into Brahman alone—the supreme substratum which is the non-dual Brahman of being, consciousness, and bliss—one shall certainly become one whose self is resolved with the conviction: "I am indeed that. (885)
This earth is neither existence nor water, nor fire, nor air, nor space, nor the collection of their effects;
it is that pure reality which serves as the substratum for these.
I am that one, supreme reality, which is truly existent. ||886||
There is no sound, no form, nor even touch;
likewise, there is no taste, nor smell, nor anything else—
that which is the pure foundation of these.
I am that one, supreme reality, the very Self. ||887||

I am that one, supreme reality, the very Self. ||888||
Neither the body, nor the senses, nor the vital breath, nor the mind, nor the intellect, nor the consciousness, nor the notion of "I" exists;
that which is the pure, eternal, one, and supreme reality, serving as the substratum of all these, that alone am I. (889)
There is no place, no time, nor even any direction; there is no other entity in the form of gross, subtle, or anything else.
That which is their pure substratum—the one, supreme, and true Being—that alone am I. (890)
That which is the substratum of this visible world, consisting of name and form, is Brahman; it is Truth, it is Being.
Whether walking, standing, or even lying down, one should always [realize this].
The wise person should perform [the practice] as interpenetrated by external objects of perception. ||891||
One should contemplate: "I am indeed Brahman—non-dual, supreme bliss, stainless through the dissolution of superimposed name, form, and so forth. (892)
I am indeed Brahman alone—unchanging, formless, stainless, free from disease, devoid of beginning and end, and complete; of this there is no doubt. (893)
One should contemplate: "I am indeed Brahman—stainless, free from fear, devoid of the three kinds of cutting (of body, speech, and mind), blissful, imperishable, and liberated. (894)
One should contemplate: "I am indeed Brahman—without distinction, without appearance, eternally liberated, changeless, the single essence of pure consciousness, and truth. (895)
One should contemplate: "I am indeed Brahman—pure, awakened, established in reality, supreme, indivisible from the inner self, self-luminous, and the universal space. (896)
One should contemplate: "I am indeed Brahman alone—the supremely non-dual, absolute, great, free from conceptual construction, and existing as mere subtle being. (897)
Thus, for one who meditates upon the object presented solely by words such as "the changeless" and so forth, the mind becomes established in the focal point (lakṣya). ||898||
Concentration is free from conceptual construction.

When the mental fluctuations, having become one with that [Self] through immersion in the essence of the bliss of Brahman, abide in an immovable state, that is *samādhi* without conceptual construction (*akalpaka*). (899)
Whether engaged in activity or remaining inactive, the ascetic, ever vigilant and with senses conquered, should always practice the sixfold concentration with great care. (900)
As long as the cognition of erroneous objects does not cease entirely,
and as long as the manifestation of one's own true nature has not become established and free from objects,
one should spend that time continuously through the sixfold samādhi.
No negligence should be practiced here by the wise person desiring liberation;
for when there is negligence, Māyā expands, just as darkness does upon the disappearance of the sun. (902)
The wise do not remain for even a moment apart from their own direct experience;
for the wise, negligence regarding that direct experience is death, not Yama.
For one who exerts effort in this samādhi, no further conceptualization exists;
even the state of being the self of all is accomplished by means of this alone.
Indeed, the state of being the self of all is absolute oneness. ||904||
The wise know that the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman is the realization of the Self as everything;
for that very one who is liberated while living, the fruit is the experience of his own bliss. (905)
That knot consisting of latent impressions, which grasps at the unreal self through notions such as "I" and "mine," dissolves;
the bondage of karma perishes through samādhi.
The realization of Brahman as the Self is held to be unimpeded. ||906||
This is the thornless path to liberation—the abiding in the state of Brahman as one's own Self—which consists in the vision of the oneness of Being for those pure-souled seekers of liberation. (907)
Therefore, you too, being vigilant and having established meditative absorptions, should thoroughly burn away the knot;
remaining disciplined, constantly immersed in the nectar-ocean of Brahman-bliss, sport and rejoice in delight. (908)
That non-conceptual samādhi, whose characteristic is immobility of mental fluctuations—those skilled in the meaning of the Yoga-śāstras call that alone "yoga. (909)
The eight limbs of yoga are restraint (yama), observance (niyama), posture (āsana), breath control (prāṇāyāma), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), and concentration (dhāraṇā). ||910||
The wise declare that meditation is indeed samādhi;
it is the restraint of the collection of the senses arising from the realization that "all is Brahman. (911)
"This is Yama"—thus it is declared that [the mind] should be practiced again and again, through a continuous flow of similar states and the rejection of dissimilar ones. (912)
For restraint is supreme bliss; it is through restraint that the wise act, so that the constant contemplation of Brahman may occur with ease. (913)
One should know that to be the true posture; any other is the destroyer of happiness.
This is because one meditates upon all states of being, such as the mind and so forth, as being none other than Brahman. ||914||
The cessation of all mental fluctuations is called prāṇāyāma;
the suppression of the manifold world is the breath known as recaka.
The mental state "I am indeed Brahman" is said to be the *pūraka* (inhalation) breath;
thereafter, the steadiness of that state is *kumbhaka*, the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇasaṃyama*). (916)

And this [state] is the torment of the vital breath for the ignorant, yet for the awakened, it is the immersion of the mind in consciousness after abandoning the sense of self in the objects of the senses. (917)
That should be known as pratyāhāra (withdrawal), which is to be practiced by those seeking liberation, because wherever the mind goes, there one perceives Brahman. 918.
The steady holding of the mind is indeed considered that supreme concentration (dhāraṇā);
it is the state of abiding in the true mode of being, "I am Brahman," through being without support. 919.
She is renowned by the word "dhyāna" (meditation), bestowing supreme bliss;
furthermore, she is so called because of her modification-free state and her nature as the form of Brahman. 920.
The forgetting of the conduct is right concentration, which is designated as meditative absorption (dhyāna).
However, while concentration is being practiced, obstacles indeed come forth with force. //921//
||45 ||Obstacles to Yoga.
Absence of the contemplation of the dawn of birth, laziness, longing for enjoyments,
fear, darkness, distraction, the vibration of vital energy, and emptiness—
these many obstacles must be abandoned by those who know Brahman. (922)
Having abandoned these obstacles, being self-controlled and free from negligence,
you ought to realize Brahman directly through steadfastness in meditative absorption.
||46 ||One's own direct experience.

Having thus understood his own true nature through the authority of the Guru’s words and through his own reasoning, he—having stilled his senses and composed his self—remained established in the Self with an immovable form in one place. (924)
Having for a long time composed his mind in its own true nature, he arose from supreme bliss and approached the Guru again with joy. (925)
The wise one, preceded by authoritative proof, spoke with a faltering voice:
"Salutations, salutations to you, O Guru, whose nature is eternal bliss! (926)
Salutations to you who are free from attachment, peaceful, and have abandoned the sense of "I";
salutations to the abode of compassion, the infinite one, whose majesty has no limit. By your glance alone, I have become non-dual Brahman itself.
What shall I do? Where shall I go? What shall I grasp? What shall I abandon?
For by me the entire universe has been filled, as if by the waters at the end of a great aeon.
In my vast ocean of blissful awakening, thousands of world-eggs appear as bubbles;
having come into being again and again through the illusory wind, they vanish once more. (929)
"O true Guru, by your grace, I am the Self whose nature is eternal bliss;
I am full, I am faultless, and I am absolute. (930)
I am the non-doer, I am the non-enjoyer, I am changeless, I am actionless;
I am indeed a mass of bliss, I am unattached, I am Sadāśiva. //931//

The exhaustion born of the heat of worldly existence, dispelled by the falling moonlight of the excellent moon that is your sidelong glance, has in an instant led me to my own state—the imperishable bliss of unbroken majesty. (932)
Whether touched by shade or heat, cold or whatever else—whether unpleasant or pleasant—that which does not touch the person at all is distinct from it. (933)
The characteristics of the witness do not touch the witness who is distinct from them;
just as the properties of a house do not affect a lamp, he remains unchanging and indifferent. (934)

Just as fire possesses the state of being a witness to an action, or as fire possesses the power of burning in iron, or as a rope has contact with an object superimposed upon it, even so is it with me, whose nature is the immutable consciousness. (935)
Having spoken thus and praised his teacher, he bowed with humility and,
for the sake of assisting one seeking liberation, asked about the matters that ought to be inquired after.
O Blessed One, please graciously explain to me in accordance with reality the characteristics of one liberated while living, of spiritual experience, and of one liberated after death (videhamukta).
||47 ||Those belonging to the seven stages.
The venerable Guru said: "I shall describe to you from the beginning the characteristics of the stages of knowledge (jñānabhūmikā),
by knowing which everything that you have asked today will be known."
The first stage of knowledge is declared to be "the desire for the auspicious" (śubhecchā);
the second is "investigation" (vicāraṇā), and the third is "the thinning of the mind" (tanumānasī). //939//

The fourth is the descent into being (sattvāpatti); after that is the one named non-attachment; the sixth is the contemplation of the nature of things (padārthabhāvanā), and the seventh is remembered as the state beyond the fourth (turyagā). ||940||

"Am I remaining here merely as a fool? I should be examined by the learned and the virtuous"—desiring [the truth] preceded by such detachment is called *śubhecchā* (the desire for the auspicious) by the wise. (941)
That engagement in virtuous conduct which is preceded by the study of the scriptures, association with the wise, and a semblance of dispassion is called *vicāraṇā*. (942)
When non-attachment toward the objects of the senses arises through investigation and virtuous aspiration,
and that [non-attachment] reaches a state of attenuation, it is called *tanumānasī*.
Through the practice of the three stages, by virtue of the mind's withdrawal from objects, when it abides in the pure self of *sattva*, that is declared to be the attainment of *sattva*. (944)
That [state] which results from the practice of the four decads and has non-attachment as its fruit, characterized by the wonder of established *sattva*, is called "Attachment" (*saṃsakti*). ||945||
Through the intense practice of the five stages, by virtue of delighting solely in one's own self, there arises a non-contemplation of both internal and external objects. (946)
The sixth stage is called the cultivation of the meaning of the words (*padārthabhāvanā*), which consists in awakening through prolonged effort prompted by another. (947)
Because of long-term practice on the six stages and because no differentiation is perceived, that state of abiding solely in one's own nature is to be known as the fourth state (turyagā). ||948||
||48 ||The characteristic of knowledge.
The non-contemplation of "this is mine" regarding all objects of perception is what the great ones, the best among the knowers of Brahman, call "waking within waking. (949)
Having realized that the succession of visible objects resides within me, who am Being-Consciousness-Bliss, the abandonment of name and form is proclaimed as the waking state. (950)
In me, the all-pervading space of consciousness, there is nothing else whatsoever apart from the nature of awakening; thus, the states of waking and sleep are said to be merely blown away. //951//
With the destruction of fundamental ignorance, there is not even the slightest bondage for me through the activities of the semblance of causes; this is declared to be like waking from a dream. (952)
When the ignorance regarding causes is destroyed, that knowledge in which the seer, the seeing, and the seen no longer exist as effects is proclaimed to be the dream of a dream. (953)
When one's own mental fluctuations, rendered motionless through extremely subtle inquiry, dissolve into pure awareness, that state is called dreaming and deep sleep. (954)
O learned one, the experience of bliss, which has entered through the expansions of mental fluctuations into cognitions whose form is consciousness, is described as "sleep" and "waking. (955)
When the state of being has long since ceased, and one abides in the arising of internal bliss, that which attains identity with the Self is called deep sleep and dream. (956)
The mental activity directed toward the visible world is the contemplation of its state of isolation;
the attainment of oneness with supreme consciousness is called the sleep of sleep. (957)
Appearing like the Supreme Brahman, unchanging and of a single form in all states, that one sustaining power is celebrated as the Fourth (turyā). 958.
Thus, reflecting upon the manifestation of these states, one who is happy is liberated.
The triad beginning with *śubhecchā* is traditionally taught as being endowed with both differentiation and non-differentiation of the stages (*bhūmi*).
When the cognition of duality has subsided as it truly is, this world is said to be "awake," once stability has been attained in non-duality and duality has come to rest. (960)
Through the excellent yoga of the fourth stage (*turya-bhūmi*), they cause the world to sleep as if in a dream;
having ascended to the fifth stage, which is named the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*).
Having attained the sixth stage, he should remain eternally inward-turned, resting solely in non-duality, with all particular aspects stilled. (962)
Due to exhaustion, one appears as if in a deep sleep; practicing on this stage, one becomes thoroughly free from mental afflictions. (963)
The king of yogis gradually attains the fourth state and the seven stages;
here, the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta) is called liberation while in the disembodied state (videhamukti). ||964||

Where there is neither non-existence nor existence, neither "I" nor even the absence of egoism—there one who has utterly exhausted all mental constructions abides in non-duality, entirely fearless. (965)
Empty within and empty without, like an empty jar in the sky;
full within and full without, like a full jar in the ocean. (966)
Even while engaged in worldly affairs, he for whom all this remains as it truly is—like the sky that has subsided yet remains—is called one liberated while living. //967//
When the light of the mind neither rises nor sets with respect to pleasure and pain, and when one's state is unattainable by others, he is called liberated while living (jīvanmukta). //968//
He who remains awake while in the state of deep sleep, for whom no waking state exists, and whose consciousness is free from latent impressions—he is called liberated while living. (969)
Even while acting in accordance with passion, hatred, fear, and the like, he who is as utterly transparent as the inner sky is called one liberated while living. //970//
He whose state of being is free from egoism, whose intellect is not stained—
whether he is acting or not acting— he is called liberated while living.
He who remains cool even while engaging in the entire web of worldly affairs, his self being as full as it is in matters for the sake of others—he is called one liberated while living. //972//
He who has found rest in an unagitated mind within the supremely purifying state of pure consciousness, free from duality, is called one liberated while living. //973//
This world, this very collection of visible objects, is unreal;
he in whose mind it does not manifest is called one liberated while living (jīvanmukta). //974//
"I am the conscious self, I am the supreme self, I am devoid of qualities, I am higher than the highest.
He who remains established in the Self alone is called one liberated while living (jīvanmukta). ||975||
"I am distinct from the three bodies; I am pure consciousness.
He within whose heart [the realization] 'I am Brahman' resides is called one liberated while living. (976)
He for whom the body and so forth do not exist, who possesses the certainty that "I am Brahman," and who is filled with supreme bliss—he is called one liberated while living (jīvanmukta). ||977||
"I am Brahman, I am Brahman, I am Brahman"—this is the certainty;
"I am consciousness, I am consciousness"—he who possesses this is called liberated while living. (978)
||49 ||Liberation while disembodied (videhamukti) ||

Having abandoned the state of liberation while living (jīvanmukti) once his own body has been surrendered to time, he attains disembodied liberation (videhamukti), just as the wind reaches a state of motionlessness.
Then that arose which is beyond the reach of even words;
that which is the Void for the proponents of the Void, and that which is Brahman for the knowers of Brahman. (980)

For those who know consciousness, it is consciousness; for those whose nature is impurity, it is the essence of impurity; for those with the Sāṃkhya view, it is the Puruṣa; and for the proponents of Yoga, it is Īśvara. (981)
Śiva is for those who abide in the path to liberation; Kāla is for those who maintain that time alone is the ultimate reality.
That which is the established conclusion of all scriptures, that which conforms to the heart of all, that which is everything and pervades all—that reality is this very one who smiles. (982)
"I am indeed Brahman; I am indeed Consciousness"—even such thoughts are not entertained.
He who remains as pure consciousness alone, bodiless, is truly liberated. (983)
He for whom there is no manifestation of conceptual proliferation, nor even the form of Brahman here,
whose state is beyond the transcendent, being bodiless— he is indeed liberated.
He who has transcended the fluctuations of the mind, who illumines the fluctuations of the mind, and who is devoid of mental fluctuations—that bodiless one is indeed liberated. ||985||
Free from all thoughts of "this is the individual self" or "that is the supreme self," with a soul devoid of all mental constructs, he is bodiless and truly liberated.

He whose nature is devoid of that which is expressed by the syllable *oṃ*, who is free from all that can be expressed, whose nature is devoid of the three states, and who is bodiless—he is indeed liberated. (987)
The slough of a snake, cast off and devoid of life, may lie fallen upon an anthill; yet the serpent does not regard it as himself. (988)
In this way, when false knowledge along with its cause has been destroyed by the fire-tuft of inward-facing wisdom, one no longer identifies with either the gross or the subtle body. ||989||
Because it is formless, this [Self] becomes bodiless through the realization of "not this, not this.
Furthermore, these three—the Viśva, the Taijasa, and the Prājña—[are likewise devoid of body]. ||990||
Virāṭ, Hiraṇyagarbha, and Īśvara—these three are the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), the individual body (piṇḍāṇḍa), and the worlds beginning with Bhūḥ, respectively. ||991||
Through the dissolution of their respective limiting adjuncts (upādhi), they dissolve into the inner self (pratyagātman).
Thereafter, all is silent; indeed, silent, silent—the Truth is nothing whatsoever.
There is no distinction of time, no distinction of substance, no distinction of place, nor any distinction of its own nature; there is not even the slightest difference whatsoever. 993.
In the statement "the individual soul and the Lord," and in the Vedic scriptures, it is said:
"I am this very consciousness," and also, "I am consciousness. (994)
Thus, he who is devoid of the body and free from all conceptual determination is indeed liberated;
in reality, whether from the perspective of the phenomenal or the absolute, only Brahman exists directly. 995.
That Brahman which is the object of that knowledge consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss;
it is peaceful, transcendent, and is called the Supreme Brahman. (996)
Indeed, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the spiritual scriptures (*adhyātma-śāstra*) is the negation of everything:
here there is neither ignorance (*avidyā*) nor illusion (*māyā*); apart from that, there is only the peaceful Brahman. (997)
Having cast off both good deeds toward those dear to oneself and evil deeds toward those who are disliked, one attains the eternal Brahman through the yoga of meditation. 998.
To whatever extent and in whatever manner everything is completely renounced by the wise one, to that same extent the supreme bliss, which is the Supreme Self alone, remains. (999)
Wherever the knower who always knows the supreme imperishable may die, he is dissolved into the supreme Brahman; for him, no departure of the vital breaths is intended.
Whatever object is held as "mine," by relinquishing that one attains liberation;
when this mind is severed by the weapon of non-conceptualization (asaṃkalpa), [then liberation is attained]. 1001.
"Then one attains Brahman, which is all, omnipresent, and peaceful.
Having heard these words of the guru, the disciple's doubts were severed. (1002)
Having known all that is to be known and having prostrated at the lotus feet of the true guru,
he, permitted by him, departed with his bonds completely severed.
This Guru, his mind perpetually immersed in the ocean of eternal bliss, wandered about peerless, purifying everything with his nectar-like presence. 1004.
Thus, through the dialogue between the teacher and the disciple, the definition of the Self has been established for the easy understanding of those seeking liberation. 1005.
This work, titled *Sarvavedāntasiddhāntasārasaṃgraha*, has been composed for the wise in order to sever the knot of the heart. (1006)
Thus [ends the work] of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda.
The *Sarvavedāntasiddhāntasārasaṃgraha*, the work of the venerable Śrī Śaṅkara Bhagavat, is complete.
Thus.
